title: Primary and secondary vasculitis of the lung - critical evaluation of the update classification.
abstract: Vasculitis in the lung can be separated into infectious and non-infectious, and in systemic and localized ones. Three major categories in the lung are known, previously named Wegener's granulomatosis, Churg-Strauss syndrome, and microscopic polyangiitis. The classification of vasculitis was proposed in 1994, including a size distribution for each type, an antinuclear and anticytoplasmic antibody profile (ANCA), and an organ location. In an updated classification (2011) the names for two of the most common primary vasculitis were replaced: Wegener`s granulomatosis by Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and Churg-Strauss syndrome by Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA). This proposal has been critically discussed in meetings of the pulmonary working group of ESP (2025) and the Pulmonary Pathology Society Meeting (Quebec, 2026). There were doubts about the usefulness of the when applied in pulmonary pathology. A new proposal is presented here. This classification is based on pattern recognition, such as neutrophilic, eosinophilic, and other forms of vasculitis. As many other types of pulmonary vasculitis were not covered in the old nor in the new proposal, several variants are added. This applies for example to vasculitis seen in autoimmune diseases. There is no doubt, that a classification of vasculitis is important, to sort the type of vasculitis. If possible, such a classification should be useful not only in lung pathology but more general in any other organ system. However, in several organ systems the clinical picture and the laboratory test allow a diagnosis, which is not the case in lung. On CT scan most types of pulmonary vasculitis present with ground glass opacitis with/without nodules. Often biopsies are labelled as interstitial lung disease.

title: Association of pre-closure intraoperative fibrinogen administration with early postoperative hemostasis in patients undergoing head-pelvic ring traction and three-column osteotomy for severe spinal deformity: a retrospective study.
abstract: Background Severe spinal deformity correction is associated with substantial perioperative blood loss. Evidence on pre-closure intraoperative fibrinogen administration in this setting remains limited. This study evaluated whether pre-closure intraoperative fibrinogen administration was associated with more favorable early postoperative hemostasis-related parameters. Methods This single-center retrospective study included 50 patients with severe spinal deformity who underwent head-pelvic ring traction followed by corrective surgery. Patients were classified into a fibrinogen group and a non-fibrinogen group according to whether they received pre-closure intraoperative fibrinogen administration. Postoperative coagulation parameters, hemoglobin (Hb) levels, drainage volume, and radiographic correction outcomes were compared between groups. Results Twenty-five patients were included in each group. Baseline characteristics, operative time, intraoperative blood loss, and radiographic correction outcomes were comparable between groups. Compared with the non-fibrinogen group, the fibrinogen group had lower postoperative prothrombin time and international normalized ratio, and higher prothrombin activity and fibrinogen levels (all P < 0.01). Hb levels on postoperative days 1 and 3 were higher in the fibrinogen group, whereas postoperative drainage volume and postoperative red blood cell transfusion volume were lower (P = 0.002, 0.036, 0.005, and < 0.001, respectively). No significant between-group difference was observed in Hb level on postoperative day 7. Conclusions Pre-closure intraoperative fibrinogen administration was associated with more favorable early postoperative hemostasis-related parameters in patients undergoing corrective surgery for severe spinal deformity. Given the retrospective design and potential residual confounding, these findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating and require validation in prospective studies.

title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis of Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer in Transrectal Ultrasound.
abstract: Diagnosing clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) using transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) remains a challenging task due to limited image contrast and the subtle appearance of malignant lesions. In this study, we propose a novel hybrid framework that integrates multi-modality and multi-task learning for csPCa classification from TRUS data. The framework leverages complementary information from B-mode and strain elastography (SE) imaging via a dual-stream encoder, enhanced by cross-modal attention gate (CMAG) modules at each level. These CMAG modules first adaptively integrate cross-modal features and then employ a gating mechanism to regulate the flow of cross-modal context into each modality-specific stream. To mitigate the scarcity of segmentation annotations, we introduce a multi-scale prototype-guided learning (MSPL) strategy, which propagates supervision signals from a small set of labeled samples to unlabeled ones by leveraging learned prototypes across multiple feature scales. This design allows the task-shared encoder to benefit from structural cues captured by the segmentation branch, even with minimal voxel-level supervision. Additionally, a context-aware multi-scale classifier (CMSC) aggregates hierarchical decoder features to further exploit the synergy between classification and segmentation tasks. The proposed method is evaluated on an in-house dataset containing 612 subjects who underwent prostate biopsy and attains favorable performance in identifying csPCa with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.86. Extensive comparative and ablation results further highlight the efficacy of incorporating cross-modal interaction, prototype-guided learning, and context-aware classification for accurate and annotation-efficient csPCa diagnosis. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/mock1ngbrd/ProstateMMTNet .

title: Giant macular hole in a female patient with X-linked Alport syndrome harboring a novel de novo COL4A5 variant.
abstract: Purpose To report a female patient with genetically confirmed X-linked Alport syndrome (AS) presenting with progressive retinal thinning and giant macular hole formation. Methods A 28-year-old woman with a history of bilateral LASIK surgery was referred for evaluation of bilateral progressive maculopathy. Comprehensive ophthalmic examinations, including optical coherence tomography (OCT) and full-field and multifocal electroretinography (ERG), were performed. Targeted next-generation sequencing of COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5 genes was performed. Results At presentation, decimal best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 0.7 in the right eye (OD) and 1.2 in the left eye (OS). The patient had no hearing loss or family history of renal or ocular disease. OCT revealed bilateral retinal thinning. During follow-up, progressive thinning of all retinal layers was observed, and a macular hole developed in OS, gradually enlarging from 546 µm at age 34 to a giant macular hole measuring 1684 µm in minimum diameter at age 39. At 37 years of age, full-field ERG demonstrated preserved rod system function with mild cone system dysfunction, and multifocal ERG showed significantly reduced macular responses bilaterally. Genetic testing identified a novel de novo heterozygous COL4A5 variant (p.Gly775Val), classified as pathogenic, confirming X-linked AS. Conclusions X-linked AS may present with progressive diffuse macular thinning and giant macular hole formation even in female patients without hearing loss or a family history. AS should be considered in the differential diagnosis of unexplained bilateral macular thinning and giant macular hole in women.

title: GSTP1 promoter hypermethylation in prostate cancer detection: current evidence, clinical positioning, and translational gaps.
abstract: GSTP1 promoter hypermethylation is one of the most consistently documented molecular alterations in prostate cancer, with high prevalence in malignant tissue and a well-established relationship with transcriptional silencing. However, despite more than two decades of biological and diagnostic investigation, GSTP1-based testing has not acquired a clearly defined stand-alone role in contemporary prostate cancer detection. This narrative review examines why extensive biological evidence has not translated into routine clinical use and where, if anywhere, GSTP1 testing might provide meaningful value within current diagnostic pathways. Evidence from prostate tissue, urine and circulating cell-free DNA is considered alongside the effects of biospecimen selection, preanalytical handling, CpG target selection, assay design and interpretation thresholds. Tissue demonstrates the most reproducible signal and has achieved partial clinical translation through multiplex testing such as ConfirmMDx, whereas urinary and blood-based approaches remain investigational. Recent urinary findings, including in men with moderately elevated PSA, are promising but remain preliminary and have not established incremental value beyond contemporary risk assessment, biomarkers and multiparametric MRI. The translational priority is therefore not to demonstrate again that GSTP1 detects prostate cancer, but to determine whether a standardised assay provides reproducible, nonredundant and clinically actionable information at a defined decision point. Future development should prioritise clearly specified target populations, analytically validated assay configurations, clinically significant prostate cancer as the relevant endpoint, and prospective evaluation against contemporary diagnostic pathways.

title: Artificial intelligence in gamma knife radiosurgery: applications in treatment planning, response prediction, and toxicity assessment.
abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being developed across the Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS) workflow, but its current applications and readiness for clinical integration remain underutilized. This narrative review examines the emerging role of AI in GKRS, with emphasis on treatment planning, outcome prediction, and post-treatment assessment. Methods A structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus was conducted through September 20, 2026 to identify studies applying learning-based AI approaches specifically to GKRS. Eligible studies evaluated AI models using GKRS clinical, imaging, or treatment-planning data, while non-GKRS and non-learning-based studies were excluded. Included studies were synthesized according to major stages of the GKRS workflow. Results AI applications were identified across tumor segmentation, isocenter selection and treatment planning, prescription and dose-distribution prediction, synthetic computed tomography generation, and plan-quality assessment. Post-treatment applications include longitudinal tumor monitoring and prediction of response, functional outcomes, and toxicity including peritumoral edema and radiation necrosis. Several models demonstrate promising performance, but the evidence remains predominantly retrospective and task-specific, with frequent reliance on single-center or small datasets and limited external or prospective validation. Conclusion AI has the potential to improve the consistency, efficiency, and personalization of GKRS by supporting specific technical and clinical decisions. Further multicenter validation, prospective evaluation, workflow integration, and demonstration of meaningful clinical benefit are required before routine adoption. AI currently remains a decision-support tool rather than a replacement for radiosurgical expertise.

title: Cardiovascular Toxicity Across the Cancer Immunotherapy Spectrum: Mechanisms and Management in Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor (ICI) and Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-Cell (CAR-T) Therapy.
abstract: Purpose of review This review evaluates the evolving landscape of cardiovascular toxicities associated with two pillars of modern cancer treatment: immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. It examines their distinct immune-mediated pathophysiologies, clinical manifestations, and management frameworks. Recent findings While ICIs carry a clinical trial incidence for cardiotoxicity of approximately 1%, real-world data suggest rates of 3-5%, with myocarditis sometimes manifesting early as part of a high-mortality "Triple M" or overlap syndrome. Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) occur in nearly 50% of ICI-myocarditis cases. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation, biomarkers and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) using the modified Lake Louise criteria, with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) detection sensitivity increasing from 21.6% to 72.0% when imaged after four days of symptoms. Conversely, CAR-T cardiotoxicity is predominantly driven by cytokine release syndrome (CRS), which affects 49-93% of patients with currently licensed products. Severe CRS more than doubles the risk of cardiovascular events, including a 6-10% incidence of LVEF decline and a 4-18% incidence of arrhythmias. Recent advancements include machine learning models to predict MACE and structured screening programs to risk-stratify candidates. Cardiotoxicity remains a significant complication, highlighting the need for vigilant monitoring and early intervention. Management relies on baseline risk assessment and rapid deployment of targeted therapies, such as high-dose methylprednisolone for ICI-myocarditis and IL-6 inhibition (tocilizumab) for CAR-T-related CRS. A multidisciplinary cardio-oncology approach is essential to mitigate risks. With early diagnosis and appropriate immunosuppressive strategies in a multidisciplinary setting, these complications can be better managed, optimising oncological benefits whilst reducing treatment-related morbidity and mortality in majority of patients.

title: Sonographic Evaluation of Plantar Hindfoot Pain in Athletes.
abstract: Purpose of review To provide an anatomy-based review of musculoskeletal ultrasound (US) in the evaluation of plantar hindfoot pain in athletes. This review summarizes normal sonographic anatomy, characteristic findings, diagnostic utility, and limitations for plantar fascia, heel fat pad, calcaneal, peripheral nerve, vascular, and foreign-body pathology. It also examines how US findings should be integrated with the history and physical examination in athletes. Recent findings Recent studies support high-resolution, dynamic US as a useful imaging modality for plantar hindfoot pain. US enables real-time assessment, contralateral comparison, sonopalpation, and evaluation during dynamic maneuvers. Emerging literature has further characterized the layered structure and loading behavior of the heel fat pad, dynamic sonographic findings of fat pad fracture and subluxation, and assessment of peripheral nerve entrapment. Recent studies also demonstrate that plantar fascia, heel fat pad, and other hindfoot abnormalities are prevalent in asymptomatic athletes. Although sonographic abnormalities may be associated with future time-loss injury, their low positive predictive value limits their role as a screening tool. MRI remains important when evaluating suspected calcaneal stress injury, marrow pathology, or complex soft-tissue disease. US is an accessible and valuable modality for the assessment of plantar heel pain in athletes. A structured, symptom-driven examination may improve diagnostic precision and identify alternative or coexisting pathology. Sonographic findings should be correlated with symptom location, physical examination, and sonopalpatory pain, particularly because structural abnormalities are common in asymptomatic athletes.

title: Deep learning-based renal-trauma classification: comparison of two-dimensional convolutional neural network and vision-transformer models on arterial- and venous-phase computed-tomography images.
abstract: Rapid and accurate detection of renal trauma is essential in emergency medicine. This study aimed to automatically classify renal trauma using 2D convolutional neural network (CNN) and vision transformer (ViT) models on arterial- and venous-phase computed tomography (CT) images. We analyzed CT images from 94 patients, including 47 without renal trauma and 47 with renal trauma (30,951 and 15,086 images, respectively). Arterial- and venous-phase CT images were reconstructed into axial, coronal, and sagittal images, with the renal regions cropped to construct the image datasets. Five pretrained CNN-based and five pretrained ViT-based 2D models were fine-tuned to classify renal trauma, and their performance was evaluated at the slice and patient levels using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity. At the slice level, the sagittal Inception-V3 model achieved the highest AUC values of 0.986 for venous-phase and 0.975 for arterial-phase images. At the patient level, the coronal Inception-V3 model achieved the highest AUC values of 0.991 for venous-phase and 0.945 for arterial-phase images. CNN-based models outperformed ViT-based models at both levels, with slice-level mean AUC values of 0.971 and 0.940 for venous-phase and 0.942 and 0.914 for arterial-phase images and patient-level values of 0.947 and 0.928 for venous-phase and 0.914 and 0.886 for arterial-phase images, respectively. The 2D models demonstrated high diagnostic performance for renal trauma, even when using arterial-phase images alone, supporting their potential for rapid decision-making in emergency settings.

title: Central Asian-Mongolian-Iranian celiac disease taskforce: A look into the future- 2026-2035 and beyond.
abstract: Background There is limited data on celiac disease (CeD) from Central Asia and Mongolia. In contrast, data from Iran shows a rapid increase in the number of diagnosed cases since early 2000s. Limited data is available and likely due to low awareness, limited diagnostic access and the current belief that CeD is uncommon. Objectives The first international Task Force for CeD met to have a look into the future at the Republican Specialized Centre of Pediatrics, Tashkent, Uzbekistan (March 2026) to (1) focus on diagnosis and prevalence research; (2) promote affordable serological testing for all socio-economic strata; (3) improve involvement of medical sub-specialties; (4) suggest proper gluten-free legislation for wheat food labeling and (5) organize affordable gluten-free food for CeD patients in general. KEY RECOMMENDATIONS (2026-2030): Standardize local tissue transglutaminase antibodies (tTGA) testing to ≤ 5-10$/test; evaluate point-of-care tests in rural clinics Conduct population-based serosurveys in Central Asia, Iran and Mongolia (n ≥ 1000 each) Advocate for mandatory gluten-free labeling standards (≤ 20 ppm) Evaluation of abdominal ultrasound in CeD recognition Establish CeD patient associations to improve patient empowerment in Central Asia, Mongolia and Iran Develop online CeD training modules for clinicians in local languages.

title: Borrelia garinii spirochetemia in a previously healthy child presenting with Streptococcus anginosus group brain abscess: a case report.
abstract: Background The clinical significance of transient Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato complex (hereafter referred to as B. burgdorferi) spirochetemia remains poorly understood and has rarely been documented. We report the isolation of viable B. garinii genospecies from the blood of a previously healthy child presenting with a Streptococcus anginosus group (SAG) brain abscess. Case presentation An eight-year-old girl presented with four days of headache, fever, nausea, slightly reduced general condition, and mild facial asymmetry. Initial evaluation, including lumbar puncture, raised suspicion of viral meningitis or Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB). Based on the differential diagnosis of Lyme disease, she was enrolled in the prospective BRILLIANT study (NCT06045416), with additional blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sampling for B. burgdorferi culture and serology. Following initial outpatient management, she re-presented with clinical deterioration and signs of raised intracranial pressure. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging revealed a brain abscess requiring surgical drainage. Abscess cultures yielded SAG. Dental treatment four days before symptom onset provided a plausible source of infectious spread. Treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole for six weeks resulted in complete clinical recovery and radiological improvement. Borrelia burgdorferi-specific two-tier serology and CSF culture remained negative. In contrast, blood plasma culture for B. burgdorferi obtained at initial presentation yielded viable spirochetes after seven weeks. Borrelia burgdorferi DNA was confirmed by flaB-targeted qPCR, and hybrid whole-genome sequencing generated a near-complete genome identifying B. garinii genospecies. Conclusion This case demonstrates viable B. garinii spirochetemia without serological evidence of LNB, incidentally detected during investigation of a SAG brain abscess. It highlights the uncertain clinical significance of transient B. burgdorferi spirochetemia, and the importance of interpreting microbiological findings within the clinical context.

title: Full-Cohort Organ Dose Assessment from Low-Dose CT Lung Cancer Screening in the National Lung Screening Trial.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Organ-specific dose estimates are needed to characterize radiation exposure from repeated low-dose computed tomography (CT) lung cancer screening in the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST). The objective was to estimate study-level doses and participant-level cumulative doses in the NLST CT screening cohort. Materials and methods This retrospective dosimetry study included 25,051 NLST CT screening participants from the Lung Screening Study and American College of Radiology Imaging Network components after excluding participants with any examination lacking a valid manufacturer-appropriate tube current-time input. Image-series metadata were linked with age, sex, height, and weight, and then valid records were grouped into 69,601 study-level screening examinations. Organ absorbed doses and effective dose were calculated using the National Cancer Institute dosimetry system for Computed Tomography with sex- and body-size-specific adult phantoms. Scan-range-related dose uncertainty was assessed with 50 stochastic simulations. Results Participants underwent a mean of 2.78 study-level screening examinations; the median study-level volume CT dose index was 3.30 mGy. Median (interquartile range) study-level lung, breast, heart wall, active marrow, and effective doses were 3.93 (3.13-4.96), 3.94 (3.14-5.04), 3.94 (3.14-5.01), and 1.26 (0.99-1.60) mGy, and 2.07 (1.65-2.59) mSv, respectively. Corresponding cumulative participant-level doses were 11.30 (8.89-14.50), 11.39 (9.01-14.75), 11.41 (8.93-14.66), and 3.63 (2.79-4.66) mGy, and 5.94 (4.69-7.64) mSv. Scan-range-related dose uncertainty was greatest for thyroid dose (mean coefficient of variation, 21.1%) and low for in-field organs. Conclusion Using NLST low-dose CT screening data, we estimated participant-level cumulative organ and effective doses and characterized variation across organs and body-size groups.

title: MRI Interpretation of Suspected Pediatric Acute Appendicitis: The Role of Pediatric Subspecialty Training.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Magnetic resonance diagnosis of pediatric acute appendicitis is highly accurate but may vary depending on reader training and subspecialty expertise. The study aims to compare the diagnostic performance of fellowship-trained pediatric radiologists and nonpediatric fellowship-trained emergency radiologists for non-contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) diagnosis of suspected pediatric acute appendicitis (AA). Materials and methods Retrospective, single-center study including 122 patients who underwent non-contrast-enhanced MRI for clinical concern of AA, following equivocal or inconclusive ultrasound. Reference standard based on clinical follow-up and surgical notes. Two fellowship-trained pediatric radiologists and two nonpediatric fellowship-trained emergency radiologists independently reviewed the examinations using a standardized yes/no case report form. Paired comparisons used McNemar's test. Predictive values are reported descriptively with 95% confidence intervals, with between-groups differences assessed using case-level bootstrap resampling. Appendix visualization was analyzed descriptively only. Results The cohort included 122 patients (63 male [51.6%], 59 female [48.4%]; median age 11 years, IQR 7-13 years, range 4-18 years), of whom 31 (25.4%) had pathology-confirmed AA. Sensitivity for MRI diagnosis of AA was similar between groups (fellowship-trained pediatric 87.1% [71.1-94.9] vs nonpediatric fellowship-trained 90.3% [75.1-96.7]; P = 1.00), with higher specificity among pediatric radiologists (97.8% [92.3-99.4] vs 84.6% [75.8-90.6]; P = 0.002). Specificity was also higher among pediatric radiologists for direct signs (98.9% [94.0-99.8] vs 86.8% [78.4-92.3]; P = 0.001) and for combined direct and indirect signs (98.9% vs 92.3%; P = 0.03), as was accuracy for MRI diagnosis of AA (95.1% [89.7-97.7] vs 86.1% [78.8-91.1]; P = 0.03) and for direct signs (94.3% vs 86.1%; P = 0.03). Positive predictive value was higher among pediatric radiologists for the diagnosis of AA, direct signs, and combined direct and indirect signs, reaching 96.2% (81.1-99.3) vs 68.4% (52.5-80.9) for direct signs (P < 0.001). Negative predictive value did not differ in any category. Interpretation time was longer for pediatric radiologists, with a median paired difference of 23.5 seconds (P = 0.04). Conclusion Fellowship-trained pediatric radiologists had higher specificity, positive predictive value, and accuracy than non-pediatric emergency radiologists for MRI diagnosis of suspected pediatric AA, with a small difference in interpretation time (median, 24 seconds). These findings, based on a limited number of readers, suggest differences in subspecialty expertise and aims and support further multicenter evaluation.

title: Preoperative respiratory muscle strength, muscle mass, and respiratory sarcopenia as predictors of postoperative pulmonary complications after thoracic and cardiac surgery: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background & aims Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) are common after thoracic, upper abdominal, and cardiac surgery and are associated with adverse outcomes. Respiratory sarcopenia (RS), characterized by coexisting reductions in respiratory muscle mass and strength, may represent a clinically relevant prognostic phenotype, but its prognostic value remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess whether low preoperative respiratory muscle mass, reduced strength, or their coexistence as RS or probable RS predicts PPCs after thoracic and cardiac surgery. Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and CENTRAL from January 1990 to February 2026 for studies relating preoperative respiratory muscle mass, strength or flow, or RS to PPCs. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality In Prognosis Studies tool. Adjusted odds ratios (ORs) were pooled using random-effects models after harmonizing effect directions such that ORs >1 denoted higher risk. Results Sixteen studies were included; all involved thoracic or cardiac surgery, and none included an upper abdominal cohort. Cutoff-based respiratory muscle strength or flow impairment was associated with increased odds of PPCs (OR 2.25, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.50-3.37; I 2 = 51.2%), with the most consistent association observed for percent-predicted peak expiratory flow (PEF) (OR 2.03, 95% CI 1.43-2.90; I 2 = 0%). Continuous PEF was associated with PPCs, whereas ultrasound-based diaphragm indices showed smaller, non-significant associations. RS or probable RS was associated with PPCs (OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.33-3.26; I 2 = 0%). Conclusions Preoperative functional respiratory muscle impairment, particularly reduced PEF, and RS or probable RS were associated with PPCs. Given that the evidence was limited, heterogeneous, and predominantly derived from thoracic surgery, prospective confirmation is needed.

title: Comparative assessment of ultrasound and bioelectrical impedance analysis for sarcopenia screening in chronic liver disease.
abstract: Background Sarcopenia, primarily defined by low muscle mass (LMM), is associated with worse clinical outcomes in chronic liver disease (CLD). Diagnosis is challenging due to the lack of standardized tools. Ultrasound (US) offers a promising method for muscle mass assessment but requires validation against reference methods like bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA). Aim To evaluate the correlation and agreement between US- and BIA-based muscle measurements and the accuracy of US in identifying sarcopenia in patients with cirrhosis and a history of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Methods In this prospective observational study, 88 patients with cirrhosis (HCC active or under follow-up) underwent muscle mass assessment by BIA and US of quadriceps and psoas muscles. Analyses included correlations, intraclass correlation (ICC), Bland-Altman plots, and ROC analysis to determine US cut-offs for sarcopenia. Results Quadriceps US indices correlated with BIA-derived ASMM/h² (r = 0.35-0.45, p < 0.01), with high inter-rater reliability (ICC 0.83-0.96). The feather index demonstrated the best discriminative ability (AUROC 0.81, sensitivity 83%, specificity 72%) in this low-prevalence setting. Dual cut-off strategies improved screening value (negative predictive values above 97%). Conclusion Muscle US is a reliable, non-invasive screening tool for sarcopenia (specifically LMM) in CLD patients. Its use can reduce reliance on complex diagnostics, enabling early detection and improved clinical management.

title: A liquid fiducial marker for image-guided proton beam therapy of abdominal tumors.
abstract: Purpose This study compared a liquid to solid fiducial markers regarding visibility, artifact characteristics on X-ray imaging and dose perturbation for image-guided proton therapy (IGPT) of abdominal tumors. Additionally, the radio-opaque composition of the liquid fiducial marker was optimized, and the chemical stability after proton beam irradiation was analyzed. Material and methods The fiducial markers inserted into an anthropomorphic abdominal phantom were exposed to X-ray, single-energy computed tomography (SECT), dual-energy CT (DECT) and cone-beam CT (CBCT) to determine contrast-to-noise ratios (CNR) and artifacts. Proton dose perturbation estimations were performed using a Monte Carlo dose algorithm. Chemical stability following proton beam irradiation was assessed with biophysical and optical methods. Results The CNR of the liquid marker with a volume ≥ 100 μl (CNR ≤ 2.69) on 2D X-ray images was superior to the solid markers (CNR ≤ 1.72). The artifact areas (A) and severity in the CT modalities were more pronounced for the solid (e.g. , sect A ≤ 279.4 mm 3 ) than for the liquid fiducial marker (A ≤ 30.5 mm 3 ). Dose mitigation of ≥ 50% in a proton beam was calculated for solid fiducial markers, while the liquid marker less influenced the dose distribution. Increasing radio-opaque content in the liquid prototypes improved visibility (CNR ≤ 2.97) without significantly increasing artifact volume (SECT: A ≤ 40.5 mm3) or dose perturbation. No degradation of the liquid fiducial marker's chemical composition was observed. Conclusion The liquid fiducial marker demonstrated comparable visibility and chemical stability with reduced artifact generation and dose perturbation compared to solid markers, indicating superiority for IGPT of abdominal tumors. Optimization of the liquid marker composition may be considered.

title: Risk-stratified Prostate Cancer Screening in 2026: Blood- and Urine-based Biomarkers.
abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) encompasses a broad biological spectrum ranging from indolent to aggressive disease. Although early randomized trials generated controversy regarding the benefits versus harms of screening, contemporary evidence supports screening and early detection strategies that focus on men at the highest risk of clinically significant PCa (csPCa) or International Society of Urological Pathology grade group ≥2. Current guidelines from major urological associations emphasize shared decision-making, with earlier screening considerations for high-risk populations. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing is important in PCa screening, but its limited specificity necessitates adjunctive tools to reduce unnecessary biopsies and overdiagnosis. Risk calculators/nomograms, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), blood-based assays (including PSA derivatives and multivariable tests such as the Prostate Health Index, 4Kscore, Stockholm3, and Proclarix), and urine-based assays (including SelectMDx, MyProstateScore 2.0, ExoDx, and miR Sentinel) further refine detection. The integration of MRI and biomarkers represents modern risk-adapted screening and early detection pathways. Ongoing large-scale trials are evaluating multimodal biomarker and MRI strategies to optimize csPCa detection while minimizing harm. Overall, risk-stratified, imaging- and biomarker-driven approaches offer pragmatic and evidence-based pathways to enhance early detection of csPCa while reducing overdiagnosis and overtreatment. PATIENT SUMMARY: This short review discusses how blood and urine tests, alongside genetic risk information, can help identify the men most likely to harbor aggressive prostate cancer-enabling early detection and intervention while avoiding unnecessary biopsies and potential harm in men at low risk.

title: The triglyceride-glucose index and intramyocardial hemorrhage identify a high-risk phenotype in STEMI.
abstract: Aims The prognostic value of combining the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index and intramyocardial hemorrhage (IMH) in STEMI is unclear. We assessed their individual and combined association with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Methods This retrospective study included 456 STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI. TyG index was calculated from admission blood samples; IMH was assessed by cardiac magnetic resonance. The primary outcome was MACE (median follow-up 4 years). Multivariable Cox regression, restricted cubic spline analysis, incremental prognostic assessment (C-index, NRI, IDI), and interaction testing were performed. Results MACE increased across TyG tertiles (15.79% → 27.63% → 43.42%). The highest tertile remained independently associated with MACE (adjusted HR 1.86; 95% CI 1.09-3.20). Patients with high TyG (≥8.66) plus IMH had the worst prognosis (HR 4.00; 95% CI 2.49-6.39; P < 0.001), far exceeding either factor alone. Adding the combined variable to a base model improved discrimination and reclassification (C-index 0.640 → 0.658; NRI = 0.216, P = 0.020; IDI = 0.025, P = 0.008). Neither additive nor multiplicative interaction was significant, and results were consistent in diabetic and non-diabetic patients. A significant interaction was observed between TyG index and infarct location (P for interaction = 0.037), with a stronger effect in anterior (HR 1.59) than non-anterior infarction (HR 0.75). Conclusions The TyG index independently predicts long-term MACE in STEMI. Combining high TyG with IMH identifies a high-risk phenotype with a 4.0-fold higher MACE risk and incremental prognostic value. originalAbstract:
Aims

The prognostic value of combining the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index and intramyocardial hemorrhage (IMH) in STEMI is unclear. We assessed their individual and combined association with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).

Methods

This retrospective study included 456 STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI. TyG index was calculated from admission blood samples; IMH was assessed by cardiac magnetic resonance. The primary outcome was MACE (median follow-up 4 years). Multivariable Cox regression, restricted cubic spline analysis, incremental prognostic assessment (C-index, NRI, IDI), and interaction testing were performed.

MACE increased across TyG tertiles (15.79% → 27.63% → 43.42%). The highest tertile remained independently associated with MACE (adjusted HR 1.86; 95% CI 1.09-3.20). Patients with high TyG (≥8.66) plus IMH had the worst prognosis (HR 4.00; 95% CI 2.49-6.39; P < 0.001), far exceeding either factor alone. Adding the combined variable to a base model improved discrimination and reclassification (C-index 0.640 → 0.658; NRI = 0.216, P = 0.020; IDI = 0.025, P = 0.008). The TyG index independently predicts long-term MACE in STEMI. Combining high TyG with IMH identifies a high-risk phenotype with a 4.0-fold higher MACE risk and incremental prognostic value. The TyG effect is stronger in anterior infarction, suggesting infarct location should be considered in metabolic risk stratification.

title: A deep learning radiomics model based on multiparametric MRI for predicting the efficacy of neoadjuvant chemotherapy in axillary lymph nodes of breast cancer.
abstract: Objectives In this study, we developed and validated a deep learning radiomics clinical (DLRC) model integrating multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) and clinical data to predict axillary pathological complete response (apCR) in cN+ breast cancer patients receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC). Materials and methods We retrospectively collected data from 221 eligible breast cancer patients. The DLRC model integrated radiomics features and deep learning scores (DL-Scores) derived from mpMRI, together with clinical risk factors, to predict apCR. Seven classifiers were employed for model construction, and the optimal classifier was selected based on classification performance to build the final model. Model performance was evaluated using the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, area under the curve (AUC), calibration curve, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Classification performance was assessed via the confusion matrix. Additionally, SHAP plots were utilized for interpretability analysis of the model. Results Multivariate analysis confirmed that progesterone receptor (PR), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), clinical T stage (OR = 0.258), and time-intensity curve (TIC) were significantly associated with apCR. The mpMRI based DLRC model achieved AUCs of 0.949 (95% CI, 0.912-0.986) and 0.932 (95% CI, 0.867-0.998) in the training and validation sets. SHAP analysis further revealed the interpretability of the model. The confusion matrix visually demonstrated the consistency between the predicted results and the true labels, validating the classification performance of the model. Conclusion The DLRC model effectively predicts apCR in breast cancer patients after NAC. It can serve as an auxiliary tool for clinicians in identifying potential candidates for axillary de-escalation, offering support for personalized precision treatment. We present this article in accordance with the TRIPOD-AI reporting checklist.

title: Atlas-assisted segment anything model for fetal brain MRI (FeTal-SAM).
abstract: This paper presents FeTal-SAM, a novel adaptation of the Segment Anything Model (SAM) tailored for fetal brain MRI segmentation. Traditional deep learning methods often require large annotated datasets for a fixed set of labels, making them inflexible when clinical or research needs change. By integrating atlas-based prompts and foundation-model principles, FeTal-SAM addresses two key limitations in fetal brain MRI segmentation: (1) the need to retrain models for varying label definitions, and (2) the lack of insight into whether segmentations are driven by genuine image contrast or merely inferred by learned spatial priors. We leverage multi-atlas registration to generate spatially aligned label templates that serve as dense prompts, alongside a bounding-box prompt, for SAM's segmentation decoder. This strategy enables binary segmentation on a per-structure basis, which is subsequently fused to reconstruct the full 3D segmentation volumes. Evaluations on two datasets, the dHCP dataset and an in-house dataset demonstrate FeTal-SAM's robust performance across gestational ages. Notably, it achieves Dice scores comparable to state-of-the-art baselines which were trained for each dataset and label definition for well-contrasted structures like cortical plate and cerebellum, while maintaining the flexibility to segment anatomical structures that could be templated by compatible atlas image and label sample pairs. Although slightly lower accuracy is observed for subtle, low-contrast structures (e.g., hippocampus, amygdala), our results highlight FeTal-SAM's potential as a flexible atlas-conditioned segmentation framework without requiring a separately trained model for each supported parcellation. This method thus constitutes a promising step toward clinically adaptable fetal brain MRI analysis tools.

title: Predicting taste alteration in head and neck cancer patients using 3D transformer-based deep learning model.
abstract: Purpose Taste alteration is a common post-treatment side effect of head and neck cancer (HNC) radiotherapy. Accurate normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) models can support treatment planning aimed at reducing side effects that impair quality-of-life. Deep learning (DL) offers opportunities to incorporate full 3D dose, CT, and organofinterest (OOI) data. Using a large prospective cohort, this study explores whether CNN and transformerbased DL models can outperform a conventional logistic regression model for predicting taste alteration 6 months after radiotherapy. Material/methods Data from 972 patients was used, with the endpoint being moderatetosevere patientreported taste alteration at six months (EORTC QLQH&N35). DL models were trained using 3D dose distributions, planning CT, OOI segmentations and clinical features. A conventional NTCP model using oral cavity mean dose, parotid mean dose, and age served as reference. Attention maps were evaluated for the transformer-based DL model to quantify the model attention to specific regions of the head and neck area. In addition, two cropping approaches for the 3D data were compared. Results The CNN and transformer DL models performed comparable to the reference NTCP model in the test set (Reference: AUC = 0.71; ResNet: AUC = 0.68; TransRP: AUC = 0.71), though calibration was best for the reference model. Shifting the crop improved DL performance and transformer attention focused on supraglottic and submandibular regions. Conclusion This study showed that the prediction of taste alteration can be achieved using DL models, particularly transformer-based models which, in contrast to CNNs, can account for global features of comprehensive 3D information of dose distribution, CT-images and organs-of-interest segmentations.

title: Systematic Review of Clinical Utility of Multimodal Imaging in Infectious Posterior Uveitis. Multimodal imaging in Uveitis (MUV) Taskforce Report 12.
abstract: Topic To systematically evaluate the clinical utility of multimodal imaging (MMI) for the diagnosis, activity assessment, longitudinal monitoring, and detection of complications in the five most prevalent infectious posterior uveitides. Design Systematic review and evidence-based quality appraisal. Participants Original research studies published between January 2018 and September 2025(primary cohort) and 2012-2017(supplemental cohort) evaluating MMI in ocular toxoplasmosis(TOXO), cytomegalovirus retinitis(CMVR), ocular tuberculosis(TB), syphilitic uveitis(SYPH), and acute retinal necrosis(ARN). Methods MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane, and Scopus were systematically searched. Independent reviewers extracted reported imaging findings and clinical utility statements for: color fundus photography (CFP), fundus autofluorescence (FAF), optical coherence tomography (OCT), fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA), indocyanine green angiography (ICGA), and OCT angiography (OCTA). Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), and certainty of evidence was graded using a bespoke consensus-based scheme informed by GRADE principles. Main outcome measures (1)reported imaging findings for each entity and modality; and (2)statements of clinical utility for diagnosis, detection of disease activity, longitudinal monitoring, and detection of complications. Results Among 122 included studies (82 primary and 40 supplemental), the primary studies contributed 5,522 individual patient examinations and 574 imaging statements, while the supplemental studies provided corroborating evidence. Overall, 366 clinical utility statements were identified across the four prespecified domains, including 30 statements supporting synergistic MMI strategies. CFP, including studies using ultra-widefield imaging, achieved high certainty for diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring in four of five entities (4/5, 80%), with moderate certainty in ARN. OCT achieved high certainty across all four clinical utility domains for four of five entities (4/5, 80%), with lower certainty in ARN owing to its limited evidence base. FFA achieved high certainty for complication detection in three of five entities. FAF achieved high certainty for disease activity in four of five entities. OCTA achieved high certainty in at least one domain for two of five entities, whereas ICGA achieved high certainty in at least one domain for only one of five entities. Conclusions Substantial evidence exists regarding the imaging findings and clinical utility of MMI in infectious posterior uveitis. Combined MMI enables integrated structural, vascular, and choroidal assessment beyond conventional clinical examination.

title: CBCT-guided plan-of-the-day adaptive radiotherapy for locally advanced cervical cancer: Feasibility and dosimetric evaluation in a resource-limited setting.
abstract: Introduction Interfractional anatomical variations during pelvic radiotherapy for locally advanced cervical cancer may compromise target coverage and increase organ-at-risk (OAR) irradiation. This study evaluated the feasibility and dosimetric impact of a cone-beam CT (CBCT)-guided Plan-of-the-Day (PoD) adaptive radiotherapy where resources are limited. Methods Twenty patients treated with definitive chemoradiotherapy were prospectively enrolled. Three volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) plans were generated for each patient using planning target volume margins of 7, 10, and 15 mm around the cervical tumour clinical target volume. Daily CBCT imaging was used to select the most appropriate plan according to daily anatomy. The workflow was implemented using standard CBCT-guided IGRT resources without dedicated online adaptive radiotherapy software. Anatomical variations were assessed over 500 treatment fractions, and dose recalculation was performed on 410 fractions. Results Substantial interfractional anatomical variations were observed. Bladder volume was lower than the planning value in 68.2% of fractions, whereas rectal distension exceeded planning values in 74.4%. The reduced-margin plan was selected in 58.8% of fractions, followed by the standard (27%) and large-margin plans (14.2%). Plan selection was significantly associated with bladder and rectal anatomical variations. Target coverage remained satisfactory across all plans (mean PTV V42.75Gy: 96.8-97.5%), with the predefined V95% criterion achieved in 85.7%, 79.8%, and 89.3% of recalculated fractions for the 7-, 10-, and 15 mm plans, respectively. Larger margins significantly increased bladder and rectal V30Gy and V40Gy values. Conclusion A CBCT-guided PoD strategy was feasible using standard IGRT resources and generally maintained high target coverage despite substantial interfractional anatomical variations. Larger margins increased OAR dose-volume parameters, supporting individualized daily plan selection where dedicated online ART infrastructure is unavailable. Implications for practice CBCT-guided PoD offers a strategy where online adaptive radiotherapy is unavailable.

title: DAG-informed analysis of muscle characteristics and overall survival in patients receiving radical treatment for bladder cancer.
abstract: Background Reduced skeletal muscle (SM) quantity and quality may influence outcomes in bladder cancer, but most studies are associative and vulnerable to confounding and inconsistent covariate adjustment. We applied a directed acyclic graph (DAG)-informed framework to evaluate associations between computed tomography-derived SM characteristics and overall survival (OS) in patients receiving curative-intent radiotherapy-based bladder preservation or radical cystectomy. Methods This retrospective two-centre cohort study included patients treated between 2014 and 2024. Computed tomography imaging closest to definitive local therapy was analysed using an automated segmentation pipeline to quantify SM quantity, expressed as skeletal muscle index (SMI), and quality, expressed as intramuscular adipose tissue ratio (IMATR). A DAG was used to prespecify the adjustment strategy, and Cox models were fitted separately within radiotherapy and surgical cohorts. Results The final cohorts comprised 353 radiotherapy-treated and 117 surgically treated patients. In the radiotherapy cohort, higher SMI was associated with improved OS (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.66-0.94, p = 0.007), while higher IMATR was associated with worse OS (HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.04-1.48, p = 0.014). In the smaller surgical cohort, point estimates were directionally discordant with the radiotherapy findings and imprecise: SMI HR 1.35 (95% CI 0.99-1.85, p = 0.057) and IMATR HR 0.86 (95% CI 0.62-1.21, p = 0.39). Conclusions In this DAG-informed analysis, higher SMI and lower IMATR were associated with improved OS in radiotherapy-treated patients. Surgical estimates were imprecise and should be considered exploratory. These findings are hypothesis-generating and support further evaluation of CT-derived muscle characteristics as prognostic markers within radiotherapy-treated populations but cannot yet establish a differential benefit for radiotherapy vs cystectomy.

title: Carcinomatous meningitis: Current insights into diagnosis, prognosis and management.
abstract: Carcinomatous meningitis, or leptomeningeal metastasis, is a severe neurological complication of solid and haematological malignancies caused by dissemination of tumour cells within the leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid pathways. Clinical presentation is heterogeneous, including headache, intracranial hypertension, cranial nerve palsies or radiculopathy, which frequently leads to diagnostic delay. Diagnosis relies on converging clinical, radiological, and cerebrospinal fluid findings, with gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spine and cerebrospinal fluid cytology remaining central despite imperfect sensitivity. Emerging tools, particularly cerebrospinal fluid circulating tumour cells and circulating tumour DNA, may improve early detection and molecular characterisation. Prognosis remains poor, with survival usually measured in months. Management should be individualised according to performance status, tumour subtype, and systemic disease control, and may combine symptomatic measures, radiotherapy, targeted systemic therapies, and, in selected patients, intrathecal chemotherapy. Early integration of palliative care remains a key component of management.

title: Artificial intelligence in diabetic retinopathy: From deep learning to foundation models, clinical translation, and real-world deployment.
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a leading cause of preventable vision impairment worldwide, with its burden increasing in parallel with the global diabetes pandemic. As a progressive microvascular disorder with neurovascular unit involvement, DR is driven by retinal ischemia, inflammation, and pathological neovascularization, while diabetic macular edema (DME) continues to represent a principal cause of vision loss. This structured narrative review provides a critical synthesis of advances in diabetic retinopathy diagnosis, retinal imaging, treatment strategies, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled screening published from January 2020 through March 2026, while selectively incorporating earlier landmark studies to provide clinical and methodological context. We summarize contemporary screening pathways and emerging retinal imaging modalities, including ultra-widefield photography (up to ~200° field of view), optical coherence tomography (OCT), and OCT angiography, examining how complementary structural and vascular biomarkers are reshaping disease severity assessment and DME characterization. We then review the evolution of AI methodologies, highlighting a transition from task-specific convolutional neural network pipelines toward transformer-based and self-supervised representation learning, including retina-specific foundation models designed to reduce annotation burden and improve robustness and generalizability under domain shift. Beyond algorithmic performance on curated benchmarks, we emphasize key translational requirements for clinical adoption, including model calibration, uncertainty-aware triage, image quality control, and external validation across imaging devices and diverse populations. Recent prospective and implementation studies across diverse healthcare systems demonstrate that the real-world effectiveness of AI-enabled DR screening depends not only on diagnostic accuracy but also on image gradability, clinically appropriate operating thresholds, uncertainty management, external validation, referral capacity, and integration with established care pathways. Evidence from the Asia-Pacific region provides important examples of these implementation challenges in heterogeneous and resource-constrained screening environments. Specific attention is given to the identification and mitigation strategies for fundus pigmentation-related performance disparities and the governance of autonomous versus hybrid human-AI screening models within evolving regulatory frameworks. Finally, we examine emerging work in oculomics for systemic risk stratification and propose a pragmatic clinical readiness framework centered on validation hierarchy, safety monitoring, and workflow integration. Particular emphasis is placed on the translational readiness of foundation models, multimodal retinal intelligence, and emerging technologies for large-scale screening, therapeutic decision-making, and longitudinal disease monitoring.

title: Peripheral exudative hemorrhagic chorioretinopathy: A comprehensive review of clinical features, differential diagnosis, pathogenesis-related disease spectra, and management.
abstract: Peripheral exudative hemorrhagic chorioretinopathy (PEHCR) is a peripheral chorioretinopathy characterized by retinal pigment epithelium detachment with either blood, exudation, or both, and may present with macular hemorrhage, macular exudation, and vitreous hemorrhage. PEHCR exhibits a variety of features on fundus fluorescein angiography, indocyanine green angiography, and ultrasound examinations. The hemorrhagic type PEHCR may greatly resemble malignant melanoma, whereas the exudative type can mimics primary vitreoretinal lymphoma making differential diagnosis of great importance. The pathogenesis may involve choroidal neovascularization. Early studies suggested a link to age-related macular degeneration, while subsequent research has revealed a close association with polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy and pachychoroid disease spectrum. Most cases of PEHCR are self-limiting and may be observed alone. For those complicated by, or at risk of, macular exudation, macular hemorrhage, as well as vitreous hemorrhage, management strategies include intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor injections, vitrectomy, laser photocoagulation, photodynamic therapy, and cryotherapy.

title: Integrative single-cell and computational pathology analyses reveal a C11orf24-associated stem-like epithelial population linked to tumor microenvironment remodeling and immune evasion in bladder cancer.
abstract: Background Cancer stem-like cells drive tumor progression and therapeutic resistance, yet the epithelial stemness hierarchy in bladder cancer (BLCA) remains poorly defined. We aimed to characterize stemness-associated epithelial populations and their clinical significance. Methods We analyzed single-cell RNA sequencing data from 92,218 cells across 13 treatment-naïve BLCA samples to characterize epithelial stemness and tumor-microenvironment interactions. Spatial transcriptomics and independent bulk cohorts were used for orthogonal and clinical validation. An HStem-associated histopathology-based prognostic model was developed by integrating quantitative image features with deep-learning representations, followed by functional validation of the candidate gene C11orf24. Results We identified a highly stem-like epithelial population (HStem) at the apex of the differentiation hierarchy, exhibiting MYC activation, oxidative phosphorylation, and DNA repair enrichment, with preferential presence in advanced-stage tumors. HStem cells were inferred to serve as major communication hubs within the TME, interacting extensively with fibroblasts and endothelial cells via MIF-CD74/CXCR4 and MIF-CD74/CD44 axes. An 86-gene HStem signature enabled development of a robust image-based prognostic model. High-risk tumors showed immune exclusion, immunosuppressive enrichment, T-cell dysfunction, and predicted checkpoint blockade resistance. C11orf24 emerged as a candidate stemness-associated regulator; C11orf24-positive cells displayed enhanced stemness and stromal interactions. Functional experiments demonstrated that C11orf24 perturbation altered clonogenic growth, migration, and invasion in BLCA cells. Pharmacogenomic analyses identified predicted therapeutic vulnerabilities that warrant experimental validation. Conclusions We identify an HStem population associated with BLCA progression, microenvironmental remodeling, and immune evasion. Integrating single-cell and spatial transcriptomics with computational pathology, we establish a clinically relevant stemness framework and identify C11orf24 as a potential therapeutic target, offering opportunities for stemness-directed precision oncology.

An HStem-associated histopathology-based prognostic model was developed by integrating quantitative image features with deep-learning representations, followed by functional validation of the candidate gene C11orf24.

Results

We identified a highly stem-like epithelial population (HStem) at the apex of the differentiation hierarchy, exhibiting MYC activation, oxidative phosphorylation, and DNA repair enrichment, with preferential presence in advanced-stage tumors. HStem cells were inferred to serve as major communication hubs within the TME, interacting extensively with fibroblasts and endothelial cells via MIF-CD74/CXCR4 and MIF-CD74/CD44 axes. An 86-gene HStem signature enabled development of a robust image-based prognostic model. High-risk tumors showed immune exclusion, immunosuppressive enrichment, T-cell dysfunction, and predicted checkpoint blockade resistance. C11orf24 emerged as a candidate stemness-associated regulator; C11orf24-positive cells displayed enhanced stemness and stromal interactions. Functional experiments demonstrated that C11orf24 perturbation altered clonogenic growth, migration, and invasion in BLCA cells. Pharmacogenomic analyses identified predicted therapeutic vulnerabilities that warrant experimental validation.

Conclusions

We identify an HStem population associated with BLCA progression, microenvironmental remodeling, and immune evasion. Integrating single-cell and spatial transcriptomics with computational pathology, we establish a clinically relevant stemness framework and identify C11orf24 as a potential therapeutic target, offering opportunities for stemness-directed precision oncology.

title: Research Progress of Low-Intensity Pulsed Ultrasound in Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder where current pharmacological and surgical interventions, including Deep Brain Stimulation, often fail to reverse neuronal degeneration or halt disease progression. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) has emerged as a novel, non-invasive neuromodulation technology with significant therapeutic potential. This review synthesizes current research on the key acoustic parameters, biological mechanisms, and clinical applications of LIPUS in PD. Unlike High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU), which relies on thermal ablation to destroy target nuclei (e.g., Vim, STN), LIPUS utilizes low-energy mechanical waves (typically <3 W/cm²) to exert non-thermal regulatory effects without damaging tissue. Mechanisms of action include the modulation of mechanosensitive ion channels (e.g., Piezo1), enhancement of neuroplasticity via brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), promotion of autophagy, and regulation of microglial phenotypes to reduce neuroinflammation. We further compare LIPUS with HIFU, highlighting the superiority of LIPUS regarding safety, reversibility, and the absence of requirement for MRI-based thermal monitoring. While preliminary clinical studies using wearable LIPUS devices indicate improvements in motor and cognitive functions, a unified consensus on optimal stimulation parameters and targeting strategies is lacking. Future research should focus on large-scale, standardized clinical trials to establish precise protocols for LIPUS as a disease-modifying therapy for PD.

title: ADHD symptom positivity and its association with medication adherence and psychiatric burden in adults with epilepsy.
abstract: Background Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms are increasingly recognized in adults with epilepsy (AwE) and may contribute to psychiatric burden, seizure-related outcomes, and treatment adherence. We therefore investigated the frequency of ADHD symptom positivity and its associations with medication adherence, psychiatric symptoms, seizure burden, and neurophysiological findings. Methods This cross-sectional study included 100 AwE and 94 healthy controls. ADHD symptoms were assessed using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS-v1.1). Anxiety and depressive symptoms were evaluated using the Beck Anxiety Inventory and Beck Depression Inventory, respectively. Medication adherence was assessed using the Morisky Medication Adherence Scale (MMAS-8). Participants were classifiedas ASRS-positive or ASRS-negative according to the six-item ASRS Part A screener. Clinical, psychiatric, electroencephalographic, and magnetic resonance imaging findings were compared between groups. Multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors independently associated with ADHD-symptom-positivity. Results ADHD-symptom-positivity was significantly more frequent in AwE than in healthy controls (50.0% vs. 25.5%, p = 0.001). Within the epilepsy cohort, ASRS-positive participants demonstrated lower medication adherence (p = 0.010), higher rates of poor adherence (70.0% vs. 48.0%, p = 0.042), higher anxiety (p = 0.002), and depression scores (p < 0.001). Clinically significant anxiety and depression were also more common among ASRS-positive participants (p = 0.027 and p < 0.001, respectively). In multivariable analysis, depression score was independently associated with ADHD-symptom-positivity (OR = 1.147, 95% CI 1.039-1.267, p = 0.007). Conclusions ADHD-symptom-positivity is common in AwE and is associated with poorer medication adherence in the between-group analysis, but this association did not remain statistically significant after multivariable adjustment, while greater psychiatric symptom burden was observed. Routine screening for ADHD-related symptoms may facilitate identification of adults with epilepsy at increased riskfor adverse clinical outcomes and support more comprehensive epilepsy care.

title: Multimodal precision diagnostics in clinical xenotransplantation.
abstract: Recent breakthroughs in pig-to-human xenotransplantation have successfully prevented hyperacute rejection of kidney, heart, liver and lung xenografts, marking a milestone long considered a critical barrier. However, these major advances also brought new challenges into focus, as immune-mediated graft injuries including antibody-mediated rejection, T cell-mediated rejection and innate immune activation have been observed in most xenotransplantation procedures to date. Detection and management of these injuries remain a critical bottleneck, as conventional histopathology and standard clinical monitoring lack the sensitivity required to identify subclinical injury early enough to guide timely intervention. This diagnostic gap underscores an urgent need for the development of advanced, multimodal precision diagnostic frameworks to enhance immune surveillance, which will be essential for standardizing clinical protocols and enabling pathogenesis-driven therapeutic intervention. This approach will inform both immunosuppressive regimens and future gene editing strategies aimed at engineering rejection-resistant porcine organs, ultimately prolonging graft survival. Broad adoption of such an integrative strategy will be essential to transition xenotransplantation from an experimental intervention into a safe, scalable and patient-centred clinical therapy. In this Review, we synthesize recent progress in xenotransplantation and position multimodal precision diagnostics as a pivotal strategy to address the remaining immunological and clinical barriers to widespread clinical implementation.

title: Carbon nanotube-induced magnetic shielding effects on 129 Xe NMR from equivariant neural networks.
abstract: Equivariant graph neural networks (EGNNs) have been successfully used in building efficient and accurate machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) for molecular dynamics (MD) and to predict nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) parameters in complex systems. In this work, EGNNs are used to fine-tune an atomistic foundation model, which serves as an MLIP for large-scale molecular dynamics simulations of xenon in carbon nanotubes. In addition, EGNNs are employed to develop a machine-learning model for the 129 Xe NMR magnetic shielding tensor, σ , enabling its direct prediction from the MLMD snapshots. Both models are data-efficient and remain accurate well beyond their training data. Using this dual-model framework, we show that xenon encapsulated in carbon nanotubes experiences a nanotube-induced, negative 129 Xe isotropic chemical shift that varies non-monotonically with nanotube diameter and depends further on temperature and Xe loading, establishing this dual-model approach as an efficient route to interpret confinement-driven 129 Xe NMR response.

title: Comparative Assessment of Orofacial Myofunction, Strength, and Quality of Life in Children With and Without Anterior Open Bite: The OMBIT Study.
abstract: Purpose Anterior open bite (AOB) is a multifactorial malocclusion frequently associated with nonnutritive sucking habits (NNSHs) and orofacial dysfunctions. However, little is known about the specific orofacial strength and endurance profile in affected children. This study evaluated myofunctional history, orofacial myofunctional status, orofacial strength, and oral health-related quality of life (OHRQoL) in children in the mixed dentition stage with AOB, compared to controls without AOB. Method Sixteen children with AOB in the mixed dentition stage ( M age = 8.2 years) and 16 age- and gender-matched controls participated in this cross-sectional study. Dental and orofacial histories were collected through parental questionnaires. Palatal and occlusal morphologies were assessed using intraoral scans. Orofacial function was examined using the Orofacial Myofunctional Evaluation with Scores (OMES) protocol and ultrasound imaging. Maximum isometric pressure and endurance of the tongue and lips were measured using the Iowa Oral Performance Instrument (IOPI). OHRQoL was assessed using the Child Oral Health Impact Profile-Ortho (COHIP-Ortho). Results Oral habits (e.g., nail biting, lip licking) were more frequently observed in the AOB group, and parental reports indicated that persistent open mouth behavior was reported more often in children with AOB. Two thirds of the participants had a history of NNSH, with similar prevalence across groups; however, AOB was associated with NNSH cessation at an older age. AOB was associated with higher anterior tongue endurance. No other significant differences were found in tongue or lip strength or endurance, OMES scores, or COHIP-Ortho scores. Conclusions The absence of group differences in orofacial strength and most endurance measures suggests that, in this sample, mixed-dentition AOB was not accompanied by generalized orofacial strength deficits. These findings support early functional screening and suggest that function-focused orofacial myofunctional therapy, rather than strength-based training, may be a relevant approach in children with AOB.

title: Ultrasound in fetal growth restriction.
abstract: Abstract Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is associated with increased perinatal morbidity and mortality. Its recognition requires differentiation from a constitutionally small-for-gestational-age (SGA) fetus. Based on the current AWMF S2k guideline, this CME review summarizes the ultrasound assessment and clinical management of suspected FGR. Accurate first-trimester dating, standardized fetal biometry, assessment of amniotic fluid volume, and detailed anatomical evaluation form the basis of diagnosis. Consensus-based criteria distinguish early FGR before 32 + 0 weeks' gestation from late FGR at or beyond 32 + 0 weeks' gestation. Multivessel Doppler assessment of the umbilical artery, middle cerebral artery, cerebroplacental ratio, and ductus venosus provides complementary information on placental resistance, fetal redistribution, and cardiovascular decompensation. Cardiotocography, including computerized analysis of short-term variation in early FGR, is used as part of multimodal surveillance and should not be interpreted in isolation. The review discusses appropriate monitoring intervals, indications for inpatient care, antenatal corticosteroids and fetal neuroprotection when preterm birth is anticipated, as well as gestational-age- and finding-dependent timing and mode of delivery. A practical clinical case illustrates the diagnostic pathway from abnormal fetal biometry to delivery planning.

title: Temporal trends in incidence, clinical characteristics and outcomes of pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis in Southern Denmark from 2009 to 2022: a retrospective population-based cohort study.
abstract: Objectives Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis (PVO) is a severe infection with increasing incidence. We aimed to describe long-term population-based temporal trends in incidence, clinical presentation, diagnostic approaches, microbiology, and outcomes. Materials and methods We conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study including 1,017 adults with multidisciplinary team-verified PVO diagnosed at a tertiary infectious diseases referral centre in the Region of Southern Denmark between 2009 and 2022. Incidence rates (IRs) per 100,000 person-years (PY) were calculated using regional population data and compared across three calendar periods (2009-2013, 2014-2018, 2019-2022). Temporal changes in clinical characteristics, microbiology, diagnostic strategies, and outcomes were assessed. Results In total, 1,017 patients were included. The crude IR increased from 4.7 per 100,000 PY in 2009-2013 to 11.0 in 2019-2022, with the largest increase among patients aged ≥70 years. Mean age and comorbidity burden rose over time. Pain was common, fever was often absent, and neurological deficits occurred in 33.5% ( n = 341). Postsurgical infection was the most frequent primary focus, and concomitant endocarditis occurred in 8.3% ( n = 84). A microbiological diagnosis was established in 64.8% ( n = 635) of cases, most commonly Staphylococcus aureus . Use of Fluorine-18 Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography/Computed Tomography ([ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT) increased over time. Median hospital stay remained 33 days. One-year mortality increased from 9.5% to 18.2%, while relapse declined, resulting in a stable composite risk of death or relapse (20.7%). originalAbstract:
Objectives

Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis (PVO) is a severe infection with increasing incidence. We aimed to describe long-term population-based temporal trends in incidence, clinical presentation, diagnostic approaches, microbiology, and outcomes.

Materials and methods

We conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study including 1,017 adults with multidisciplinary team-verified PVO diagnosed at a tertiary infectious diseases referral centre in the Region of Southern Denmark between 2009 and 2022. Incidence rates (IRs) per 100,000 person-years (PY) were calculated using regional population data and compared across three calendar periods (2009-2013, 2014-2018, 2019-2022). Temporal changes in clinical characteristics, microbiology, diagnostic strategies, and outcomes were assessed.

Results

In total, 1,017 patients were included. The crude IR increased from 4.7 per 100,000 PY in 2009-2013 to 11.0 in 2019-2022, with the largest increase among patients aged ≥70 years. Mean age and comorbidity burden rose over time. Pain was common, fever was often absent, and neurological deficits occurred in 33.5% (n = 341). Postsurgical infection was the most frequent primary focus, and concomitant endocarditis occurred in 8.3% (n = 84). A microbiological diagnosis was established in 64.8% (n = 635) of cases, most commonly Staphylococcus aureus. Use of Fluorine-18 Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography/Computed Tomography ([18F]FDG-PET/CT) increased over time. Median hospital stay remained 33 days. One-year mortality increased from 9.5% to 18.2%, while relapse declined, resulting in a stable composite risk of death or relapse (20.7%).

Conclusions

The incidence of PVO increased markedly from 2009 to 2022, predominantly in older patients with comorbidities. Despite improved diagnostics, microbiologically-negative cases remain frequent. Mortality remained high and increased over time.

title: Clinical features associated with HFUS-defined vascular occlusion after hyaluronic acid facial injections: a retrospective exploratory study.
abstract: Hyaluronic acid (HA) filler injections are widely used in aesthetic treatments but can cause vascular occlusion. Early diagnosis is often delayed due to reliance on clinical experience. High-frequency ultrasound (HFUS) offers a noninvasive diagnostic method. The study aims to explore the association between clinical warning signs and HFUS-defined vascular occlusion after HA filler injections. This retrospective study analyzed 57 patients with suspected vascular occlusion after HA filler injections. HFUS and a clinical scoring system covering seven symptom categories were used for early evaluation. Occlusion and non-occlusion groups were compared using HFUS and clinical scores. Among 57 clinically suspected cases, 42 (73.7%) were classified as HFUS-defined vascular occlusion and 15 (26.3%) were classified as non-occlusion. In multivariable analysis, skin color change (OR 30.390, 95% CI: 2.482-372.039; p = .008) and delayed capillary refill time (OR 185.936, 95% CI: 2.638- 13,095.200; p = .016) were associated factors of vascular occlusion. A two-variable model incorporating there two features yielded an AUC of 0.944 (95% CI: 0.891-0.998). Skin color change and delayed capillary refill time were associated with HFUS-defined vascular occlusion in this exploratory cohort. These findings may help inform clinical assessment but require prospective validation in independent populations.

title: AnF-DiffPET: anatomy- and frequency-guided diffusion for simulated low-dose PET/CT denoising.
abstract: Objective. Positron emission tomography (PET) provides essential functional information for disease assessment. However, reducing injected activity or acquisition time produces low-dose (LD) PET with stronger count-dependent noise and less reliable uptake quantification. Diffusion models offer a promising solution for PET denoising by progressively recovering high-dose (HD) PET images from LD inputs. However, LD-to-HD PET denoising remains challenging because of limited anatomical guidance, unstable multi-scale feature propagation, and inaccurate recovery of uptake patterns in the frequency domain. Approach. We propose AnF-DiffPET, an anatomy- and frequency-guided diffusion framework for computed tomography (CT)-conditioned LD PET denoising. The framework integrates anatomical-frequency guidance, Multi-Scale Cross-Transformer Reconstruction, and Frequency-Contrastive Hard Mining to enhance anatomy-aware feature modulation and frequency-domain consistency during denoising. Main results. Experimental results across four simulated LD PET/CT datasets show that the proposed method improves image fidelity, anatomical consistency, and quantitative fidelity over representative CNN-based, GAN-based, Transformer-based, Mamba-based, and diffusion-based methods. Significance. AnF-DiffPET provides a PET/CT-specific diffusion restoration framework that combines anatomical guidance, multi-scale feature reconstruction, and frequency-domain regularization for LD PET denoising. The code and trained models will be publicly released upon acceptance.
