title: Longitudinal intratumoral and peritumoral MRI radiomics for predicting pathologic complete response to neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy in locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma: a retrospective two-center study
abstract: Abstract Background Pathologic complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy (NACI) is an important marker of treatment sensitivity in locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), but reliable preoperative prediction remains challenging. This study investigated whether longitudinal intratumoral and peritumoral MRI radiomics could improve pCR prediction and whether integration with clinicopathologic factors provided additional value. Methods This retrospective two-center study included 310 patients with locally advanced HNSCC who underwent NACI followed by definitive surgery, comprising 151 patients in the training cohort, 66 in the internal validation cohort, and 93 in the independent external test cohort. MRI was performed before treatment and after the second NACI cycle. Radiomic features were extracted from contrast-enhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted images within the primary tumor and 1-, 3-, and 5-mm peritumoral regions. Features were selected using reproducibility assessment, correlation analysis, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression. Pre-treatment intratumoral, on-treatment intratumoral, longitudinal intratumoral, multiscale longitudinal peritumoral, spatiotemporal radiomics, and clinical-spatiotemporal radiomics models were sequentially developed. Performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration analysis, decision curve analysis, and incremental discrimination metrics. Results Overall, 124 of 310 patients (40.0%) achieved pCR. The clinical-spatiotemporal radiomics model (M6), integrating histologic grade, combined positive score, longitudinal intratumoral features, and 3-mm longitudinal peritumoral features, showed the highest observed discrimination. The AUCs were 0.928 (95% CI, 0.882–0.974), 0.856 (95% CI, 0.749–0.963), and 0.864 (95% CI, 0.780–0.948) in the training, internal validation, and external test cohorts, respectively. In the external test cohort, sensitivity was 0.857 and specificity was 0.845. M6 also showed favorable calibration and net benefit across a broad range of threshold probabilities. Conclusions Integrating longitudinal intratumoral and peritumoral MRI radiomics with clinicopathologic factors improved preoperative prediction of pCR after NACI in locally advanced HNSCC. The model showed consistent performance in independent external testing and may support individualized pCR risk stratification, warranting further prospective multicenter validation.

title: ‘One shunt fits all?’: A comparative laboratory study of antibiotic- impregnated shunt catheters with retrospective clinical correlation
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Several antibiotic-impregnated shunt catheters are commercially available, but direct comparative data on their biochemical and physical characteristics remain limited. Previous observations from our single-centre neurosurgical unit suggested that nominally similar catheter types may be associated with different rates of otherwise unexplained abdominal pain. We therefore conducted a prospective comparative study to investigate potential biochemical and physical differences between commercially available antibiotic-impregnated shunt catheters. Methods: Ares®, Bactiseal® and XABO® catheters were compared for antibiotic content, rifampicin degradation products, elution characteristics and antimicrobial activity. Antibiotic elution was assessed during continuous saline perfusion at 20 mL/h and 37°C over 8 weeks, while antimicrobial activity against Staphylococcus epidermidis was evaluated over 60 days. Catheter dimensions, elastic modulus and surface morphology were assessed using three-dimensional computed tomography, nanoindentation and scanning electron microscopy, respectively. An exploratory retrospective quality-improvement dataset from our single-centre unit was additionally analysed to compare the frequency of otherwise unexplained abdominal pain between catheter types. Results: The three catheter systems showed product-specific differences in antibiotic content, rifampicin degradation profiles, elution characteristics, antimicrobial activity, dimensions, mechanical properties and surface morphology. XABO® most closely matched the declared antibiotic concentrations and retained the greatest proportion of intact rifampicin, while Ares® demonstrated the highest sustained clindamycin elution. All three catheters retained measurable activity against Staphylococcus epidermidis for 60 days, with XABO® showing the largest numerical inhibition zones throughout. In the 395-patient retrospective clinical analysis, otherwise unexplained abdominal pain was recorded in 90/182 patients with Ares® catheters (49.5%) compared with 12/108 patients with Bactiseal® catheters (11.1%). After adjustment for age, sex, primary diagnosis, modified Rankin Scale score and activity level, Ares® remained associated with greater odds of abdominal pain than Bactiseal® (adjusted OR 6.89, 95% CI 2.58–18.43; p<0.001). Conclusion: Commercially available antibiotic-impregnated shunt catheters showed product-specific biochemical and physical variation, while catheter type was associated with different rates of otherwise unexplained abdominal pain in a retrospective single-centre analysis. These findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish causality or clinical superiority. Prospective multicentre studies are required to determine whether catheter-specific properties translate into clinically meaningful differences and should influence individualised shunt selection.

title: Bounded Repair Reachability of Residual Critical Blocks in 3D Binary Masks under SAFE-Gated Single-Voxel Flips
abstract: Abstract Critical configurations in three-dimensional binary images violate digital well-composedness, and voxel repairs can conflict with path constraints and foreground preservation. We formulate bounded repair reachability under single-voxel flips preserving the homotopy type of the foreground complex. We establish relations among admissible path sets and show that, under flip-once, endpoint and pathwise fidelity yield identical successful instances and shortest successful depths. Breadth-first search distinguishes found repairs, bounded absence and resource-limited outcomes. On 680 residual blocks from 222 Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) 2021 masks, unrestricted searches within radius 2 and depth 6 find repairs for 72 blocks under endpoint fidelity and 15 under pathwise fidelity. An endpoint-faithful witness temporarily removes and restores input foreground; a completed search excludes pathwise-faithful repair of that block within these bounds. These results distinguish the topological validity of moves from the admissibility of repair paths. Conclusions are limited to the stated windows, horizons and moves.

These results distinguish the topological validity of moves from the admissibility of repair paths. Conclusions are limited to the stated windows, horizons and moves.

title: ASFNR Clinical State of Practice Statement on Imaging of Chronic Subdural Hematoma.
abstract: Background The efficacy of middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAE) for chronic subdural hematoma (cSDH) has heightened interest in imaging biomarkers that may reflect neomembrane activity, predict recurrence, and identify patients most likely to benefit from treatment. Characterization of hematoma internal architecture, referred to as the imaging phenotype, may provide indirect information regarding the biological activity and maturation of the neomembrane. However, imaging phenotype has not been incorporated into randomized trials or validated treatment-selection algorithms, and standardized definitions and reporting remain lacking. Methods The American Society of Functional Neuroradiology Clinical Practice Committee developed this State of Practice statement through expert consensus and review of the available literature. Key message Noncontrast CT (NCCT) remains the primary imaging modality for cSDH assessment. Hematoma burden should be characterized by maximum thickness measured perpendicular to the inner table, midline shift, and, when appropriate, volume. Volume may be estimated using the ABC/2 formula, whereas segmentation is more accurate for irregular, crescentic, or multiloculated collections when available. Internal architecture should be described using the Nakaguchi framework of homogeneous, laminar, separated, and trabecular phenotypes, with mixed or transitional features explicitly reported. Advanced techniques, including dual-energy CT, photon-counting CT, MRI, and arterial spin labeling, may provide information regarding membrane activity but are supported by limited, largely single-center evidence and currently have a problem-solving rather than routine role. Standardized reporting and prospective validation are needed before imaging phenotype or advanced-imaging biomarkers can guide treatment selection.
originalAbstract:
Background

The efficacy of middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAE) for chronic subdural hematoma (cSDH) has heightened interest in imaging biomarkers that may reflect neomembrane activity, predict recurrence, and identify patients most likely to benefit from treatment. Characterization of hematoma internal architecture, referred to as the imaging phenotype, may provide indirect information regarding the biological activity and maturation of the neomembrane. However, imaging phenotype has not been incorporated into randomized trials or validated treatment-selection algorithms, and standardized definitions and reporting remain lacking.

Methods

The American Society of Functional Neuroradiology Clinical Practice Committee developed this State of Practice statement through expert consensus and review of the available literature.

Key message

Noncontrast CT (NCCT) remains the primary imaging modality for cSDH assessment. Hematoma burden should be characterized by maximum thickness measured perpendicular to the inner table, midline shift, and, when appropriate, volume. Volume may be estimated using the ABC/2 formula, whereas segmentation is more accurate for irregular, crescentic, or multiloculated collections when available. Internal architecture should be described using the Nakaguchi framework of homogeneous, laminar, separated, and trabecular phenotypes, with mixed or transitional features explicitly reported. Advanced techniques, including dual-energy CT, photon-counting CT, MRI, and arterial spin labeling, may provide information regarding membrane activity but are supported by limited, largely single-center evidence and currently have a problem-solving rather than routine role. Standardized reporting and prospective validation are needed before imaging phenotype or advanced-imaging biomarkers can guide treatment selection.

title: Synchronous Leiomyomas of the Sigmoid Colon and Ileocecal Valve Presenting as Colonic Polyps in a Young Male.
abstract: Abstract Gastrointestinal (GI) leiomyomas are rare benign smooth muscle tumors, most commonly arising in the esophagus and stomach. Their occurrence in the colon is uncommon, and synchronous involvement of multiple colonic sites is exceedingly rare. We report a case of a young male who underwent colonoscopic evaluation for GI symptoms, which revealed polypoidal lesions in the sigmoid colon and at the ileocecal valve. Both lesions were endoscopically resected. Histopathology with immunohistochemistry is essential for accurate diagnosis and to differentiate these lesions from GI stromal tumors. Recognition of this entity is important to guide appropriate management and avoid overtreatment.

title: Biochemical-sonographic Correlations in First-trimester Screening for Foetal Aneuploidy: A Cross-sectional Study from Eastern India.
abstract: Background Aneuploidy screening constitutes an essential component of routine prenatal care worldwide, which is done by ultrasonography during the first trimester. Moreover, pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A) and free β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) reflect placental function, which serve as important biochemical markers for aneuploidy risk assessment. Aim The present study investigated the correlation between maternal serum PAPP-A and free β-hCG levels with first-trimester ultrasound screening markers, i.e. nuchal translucency (NT) thickness and nasal bone (NB) for detecting fetal aneuploidy. Materials and methods This was a cross-sectional observational study, which enrolled 139 women with singleton pregnancies at 11-14 weeks of gestation. First-trimester ultrasonography was performed by an experienced doctor, and maternal serum PAPP-A and free β-hCG were also measured. Correlation investigation was done by Spearman's correlation coefficient, while associations were done by Fisher's exact test. Results A significant positive correlation was observed between PAPP-A gestational age and maternal body mass index. Further, there were a strong negative correlation of NT thickness with PAPP-A multiples of the median (MoM) (P < 0.001) and a strong positive correlation with β-hCG MoM (P < 0.001). The fetal NB was absent in seven (5.0%) pregnancies, of which three were confirmed to have chromosomal abnormalities by noninvasive prenatal testing. Absent NB demonstrated 42.9% sensitivity and 100% specificity, while β-hCG levels were significantly higher in NB-negative pregnancies (P < 0.01). Conclusions The combined assessment of PAPP-A, free β-hCG, NT thickness, and fetal NB could improve the performance of first-trimester screening for fetal aneuploidy, enabling more accurate early prenatal risk stratification and facilitating timely clinical decision-making.

title: When Erectile Dysfunction Therapy Clouds the Vision: Central Serous Chorioretinopathy after Sildenafil in a Healthy Male.
abstract: Abstract Central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR) is a pachychoroid-spectrum disorder characterized by serous neurosensory retinal detachment secondary to choroidal vascular congestion and retinal pigment epithelial dysfunction. While corticosteroid use and psychological stress are well-established risk factors, phosphodiesterase type-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil citrate, widely used for erectile dysfunction, have been increasingly recognized as an under-reported pharmacological trigger, with proposed mechanisms involving acute choroidal vasodilation and hyperpermeability. A 39-year-old previously healthy male presented with sudden, painless diminution of vision in the right eye of 48 h, occurring shortly after ingestion of a single large recreational dose of sildenafil citrate. Best-corrected visual acuity was reduced to 6/18 in the right eye, with a normal left eye. Fundus examination revealed a well-demarcated serous macular elevation, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) confirmed a dome-shaped neurosensory detachment with a markedly elevated central subfield thickness. A comprehensive systemic and hematological workup, including thrombophilia screening and cardiac evaluation, was unremarkable, supporting a diagnosis of sildenafil-induced CSCR. The patient was managed conservatively with topical nepafenac, topical Flurbiprofen, and oral alcaftadine, along with cessation of further sildenafil use. Serial follow-up over approximately 2 months demonstrated progressive resolution of subretinal fluid, normalization of central subfield thickness, and preservation of visual acuity, with OCT angiography confirming adequate perfusion and no neovascular complication. This case reinforces sildenafil as a potential, dose-related precipitant of acute CSCR even after a single high dose in patients without conventional risk factors. Prompt recognition, drug cessation, and conservative management resulted in complete anatomical and visual recovery, highlighting the importance of a thorough medication history in young patients presenting with unexplained central visual disturbance.

title: Preoperative apical margin risk estimation from T2-weighted MRI radiomics in prostate cancer with MRI-visible apical tumors: toward multidisciplinary decision support.
abstract: This retrospective study developed and validated a T2-weighted imaging (T2WI)-based radiomics model for preoperative prediction of apical positive surgical margins (PSMs) in patients undergoing radical prostatectomy for prostate cancer. Overall, 235 patients (74 with apical PSMs and 161 without apical PSMs) were randomly divided into a training set (n = 164; 69.8%) and an independent test set (n = 71; 30.2%). Eligible patients had preoperative multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging within 6 weeks before surgery, an index lesion involving or abutting the prostatic apex, definitive apical margin status, and standard radical prostatectomy without nerve-sparing. Patients with inadequate imaging for apical assessment or region-of-interest delineation, prior transurethral resection of the prostate, or neoadjuvant androgen-deprivation therapy were excluded. A total of 1409 radiomic features were extracted from T2WI. After normalization and removal of highly correlated features (|r| > 0.99), six optimal features were selected by recursive feature elimination. A gradient boosting machine model was constructed, and performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), Brier score, and decision curve analysis. The apical PSM rate was 31.5%. In the test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.874, Brier score of 0.120, accuracy of 87.3%, sensitivity of 81.8%, and specificity of 89.8%. Skewness was the most important feature, contributing 34.8% to the model. Apical PSMs were significantly associated with extraprostatic extension (P = 0.001), and the tumor-margin model provided the greatest net clinical benefit. T2WI-based radiomics may support individualized preoperative risk assessment and surgical planning for prostate cancer.

title: Whole-body MRI with DWIBS and choline PET/CT for detecting oligoprogressive castration-resistant prostate cancer recurrence.
abstract: The diagnostic options for patients with advanced prostate cancer have expanded with the development of next-generation imaging modalities. These include whole-body magnetic resonance imaging (WB-MRI) with diffusion-weighted whole-body imaging with background body signal suppression (DWIBS) and molecular positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) using choline or prostate-specific membrane antigen radiotracers. Such modalities improve the detection of whole-body nodal and bony metastases in patients with advanced prostate cancer. A 63-year-old man with castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) underwent stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) targeting two pelvic nodal metastases identified by WB-MRI with DWIBS and subsequently confirmed by 11 C-choline PET/CT. This case highlights the potential role of 11 C-choline PET/CT and corresponding local treatment in the management of oligoprogressive CRPC.

title: Optimising neural contrast and minimising tissue shrinkage in dragon lizard brains: buffered Lugol's iodine versus phosphotungstic acid for contrast-enhanced μCT
abstract: Contrast-enhanced micro-computed tomography (μCT) has become a valuable tool for addressing neuroanatomical questions that previously required destructive histology. As a relatively new technique, it remains subject to ongoing technical refinement, and taxon- and tissue-specific protocol optimisation. We evaluated the performance of two common contrast-enhancing agents, buffered Lugol's iodine and phosphotungstic acid (PTA) in aqueous solution, for μCT visualisation of the nervous system in the Jacky dragon lizard, Amphibolurus muricatus by comparing staining time, contrast specificity and brain tissue shrinkage evaluated at three concentrations (1.25%, 2.5% and 5%). Buffered Lugol's iodine outperformed aqueous PTA by requiring shorter staining times (as short as four days) and providing better white matter-grey matter differentiation, whereas PTA required longer incubation periods of approximately three weeks and produced poorer white-grey matter differentiation. Importantly, buffered Lugol's iodine produced higher brain-to-endocast occupancy estimates than aqueous PTA, suggesting substantially reduced tissue shrinkage. PTA-treated specimens exhibited an estimated 13.3% reduction in occupancy and approximately 20% greater brain tissue shrinkage than buffered Lugol's-treated specimens. Together, these findings demonstrate that buffered Lugol's iodine staining provides the high level of internal tissue contrast required to resolve fine-scale neuroanatomical organisation in three dimensions, preserves the spatial relationships among anatomical structures, and reduces artefacts, all of which result in a closer correspondence between the brain and endocranial cavity. From a practical perspective, the study provides guidance for contrast agent selection in future μCT studies and reveals that buffered Lugol's iodine is better suited to fine-scale neuroanatomical, volumetric and geometric morphometric analyses, whereas PTA is advantageous for applications prioritising general soft-tissue or musculoskeletal visualisation.

title: Tracheal Eccentricity is Associated with Respiratory Morbidity and Mortality in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
abstract: Background Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by airway remodeling, which may affect tracheal morphology. However, the relationship between tracheal morphometry and COPD severity, quality of life, functional capacity, and mortality remains poorly understood. Objective To investigate the associations between CT-derived tracheal lumen eccentricity and clinical outcomes in COPD. Methods We analyzed data from 8,383 participants in the multicenter COPDGene study. Tracheal lumen eccentricity (ε) was calculated at each cross-section using the major and minor axes lengths and deriving final value using the arithmetic mean across all tracheal slices, where ε = 0 represents a circle and ε > 0 indicates an ellipse. Baseline assessments included spirometry measurements, 6-minute walk distance (6MWD), St. George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ), and the modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) dyspnea score. Longitudinal assessments included annualized lung function change and all-cause mortality. Multivariable models were used to evaluate associations between tracheal eccentricity and clinical outcomes. Results Tracheal eccentricity increased with severity of airflow obstruction (0.60±0.07, 0.61±0.07, 0.62±0.07, 0.64±0.08, and 0.64±0.08 in GOLD stages 0 through 4, respectively). Higher tracheal eccentricity was independently associated with lower FEV 1 (β = −0.30 L, 95% CI: −0.47 to −0.14, p<0.001), lower FEV 1 /FVC (β = −0.06, 95% CI: −0.09 to −0.04, p<0.001), lower 6MWD (β = −15.7 m, 95% CI: −25.2 to −6.2, p=0.001), higher SGRQ score (β = 16.9, 95% CI: 11.2 to 22.5, p<0.001), higher mMRC dyspnea score (β = 0.4, 95% CI: 0.1 to 0.6, p=0.007), and accelerated lung function decline (β = −23.8 ml/year, 95% CI: −2.48 to −45.13, p=0.029). Increased tracheal eccentricity is associated with increased all-cause mortality (adjusted HR: 1.81 [95% CI, 1.01-3.26]; p = 0.047). Conclusions These findings suggest that tracheal morphology may serve as an imaging biomarker for COPD outcomes, supported by significant associations with lower quality of life, lung function decline, and all-cause mortality.

title: APOE ε4 Modifies the Association of Left Atrial Remodeling With Brain Aging
abstract: INTRODUCTION Whether APOE ε4 modifies relationships between subclinical cardiac phenotypes and brain structure is unknown. METHODS In Framingham Heart Study Offspring participants, we related antecedent echocardiographic remodeling (Examinations 4–6) to repeated brain MRI, and cardiac magnetic resonance phenotypes to regional cortical morphometry, testing cardiac × APOE ε4 interactions with false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction and permutation testing of the regional screen. RESULTS APOE ε4 modified the association between antecedent left atrial (LA) remodeling and subsequent lateral ventricular expansion (β=−0.00858, P=1.45×10⁻⁴, q=0.0023; N=1,305; 3,787 MRI observations), the only FDR-significant result of 16 longitudinal tests, including with participant-specific MRI-time slopes (q=0.034); it weakened when intracranial volume × MRI time was modeled. Four regional ventricular cardiac × APOE ε4 interactions met within-family FDR criteria, but their number was consistent with chance (permutation P=0.70). Maximum LA volume index showed an APOE ε4-dependent association with left middle-occipital cortical-thickness variability (whole-brain q=0.017; permutation P=0.041) that persisted after ventricular adjustment. Cardiac phenotypes and trajectories showed no FDR-significant APOE ε4-dependent associations with plasma Aβ42/40, p-tau181, GFAP, or NfL, and adjustment for these biomarkers changed the regional interactions by at most 3.2%. Allen Human Brain Atlas data showed cholesterol-biosynthesis enrichment in the right superior frontal cortex, implicated by the LV end-systolic volume interaction, but without convergent pathway evidence. DISCUSSION APOE ε4 modified atrial–brain relationships, with the strongest evidence linking antecedent atrial remodeling to later ventricular expansion. Replication with prespecified models is needed. Highlights APOE ε4 modified how left atrial remodeling related to later brain ventricle growth. It was the only FDR-significant result of 16 tests and persisted with random slopes. In ε4 carriers, larger LA volume tracked lower occipital thickness variability. Whether APOE ε4 modifies relationships between subclinical cardiac phenotypes and brain structure is unknown.

title: MRI-Trackable Mesenchymal Stem Cells for Oncolytic Therapy: A Clinically Feasible Dual-Labeling Protocol
abstract: Non-invasive imaging of oncolytic virus-loaded mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) could help evaluate cell trafficking and delivery in cancer therapy. Labeling MSCs with iron oxide particles (IOPs) enables in vivo tracking using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This study evaluated a dual-labeling strategy that loads MSCs with MegaPro IOPs and the oncolytic virus Delta-24-RGD (DNX-2401; tasadenoturev) and assessed cellular function and MRI detectability. MSCs were labeled with IOPs alone or in combination with the oncolytic virus. We compared cell viability and intracellular iron content among IOP-labeled, dual-labeled, and naïve MSCs, and evaluated differentiation, invasion, and immunophenotype in naïve and IOP-labeled MSCs. We evaluated phantoms containing varying numbers of IOP-labeled MSCs (9 × 10³–1.5 × 10 5 cells) using R2-, R2*-, and R1-weighted MRI, and generated corresponding relaxation rate maps to assess concentration dependent contrast and detection sensitivity. Iron content was comparable between IOP-labeled and dual-labeled MSCs (9.2 ± 2.6 and 11.6 ± 1.4 pg/cell, respectively), with >91% viability across all groups. IOP-labeled MSCs retained invasion and differentiation potential. At the highest labeled-cell concentration, R2*, R2, and R1 increased approximately 4, 2.5, and 1.5 fold, respectively, relative to the agarose control. The estimated detection limits were approximately 2 × 10³ cells for R2* and 6 × 10³ cells for R2 and R1. These findings demonstrate that dual labeling of MSCs with IOPs and oncolytic virus preserves key cellular characteristics while providing MRI-detectable contrast, supporting further investigation of this approach for image-guided tracking of cell-based cancer therapies.

title: Pharmacologic inhibition of OLIG2 by CT-179 disrupts mitotic progression and enhances standard-of-care chemoradiotherapy in glioblastoma
abstract: Background Glioblastoma (GBM) remains uniformly fatal. The basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor OLIG2 is universally expressed in diffuse glioma, sustains the tumor-propagating stem-like fraction, and opposes p53-mediated genotoxic responses, but has historically been considered undruggable. We characterized CT-179, a brain-penetrant small-molecule OLIG2 inhibitor, as a candidate therapeutic for GBM. Methods Target engagement was assessed by cellular thermal shift assay, differential scanning fluorimetry, crosslinking, and electrophoretic mobility shift assay. Anti-tumor activity was evaluated across eleven patient-derived GBM cell lines, in zebrafish oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC)-derived tumors, and orthotopic and subcutaneous GBM models, including combinations with radiotherapy plus temozolomide and with selective Bcl-2 family inhibitors. Results: : CT-179 engaged OLIG2 and altered the conformation of dimerized OLIG2 on chromatin without preventing dimerization or fully displacing OLIG2 from DNA. CT-179 reduced OLIG2-positive OPC’s and OPC-derived tumors in zebrafish and inhibited proliferation across all eleven GBM lines (IC50 < 360 nM), depleting the stem-like fraction and inducing apoptosis through mitotic catastrophe, mitotic slippage, or a hybrid response. RNA-seq across three patient-derived glioma stem cell lines identified β-tubulin gene isoforms as the most strongly CT-179-down-regulated transcripts at the early time point and showed correlated β-tubulin and OLIG2 expression in TCGA glioblastoma specimens. Combination with the Mcl-1 inhibitor S63845 or the Bcl-2/Bcl-xL/Bcl-w inhibitor ABT-737 produced greater-than-additive cytotoxicity. Oral CT-179 crossed the blood-brain barrier and extended median survival as a single agent across two independent adult orthotopic patient-derived backgrounds (GBM8 and G06); intraperitoneal CT-179 was associated with reduced intratumoral OLIG2 and Ki-67 staining in GBM8 orthotopic xenografts. Combination of CT-179 with radiotherapy and temozolomide eliminated all GBM8 and 7 of 8 GBM4 subcutaneous xenografts without weight loss and significantly extended survival when combined with radiotherapy in MGMT-unmethylated GBM6 orthotopic xenografts (CT-179 administered intraperitoneally). Conclusions CT-179 is a brain-penetrant inhibitor of an established GBM driver with single-agent and combination activity across several orthotopic models, supporting clinical development for GBM and translational evaluation in other OLIG2-dependent CNS malignancies. Key Points CT-179 is the first brain-penetrant small-molecule inhibitor of OLIG2 with potent activity across patient-derived glioblastoma models. CT-179 induces apoptosis through mitotic catastrophe and slippage rather than collapse of receptor tyrosine kinase signaling. Oral CT-179 combined with radiotherapy and temozolomide eliminates the great majority of subcutaneous patient-derived GBM xenografts without overt toxicity. Oral CT-179 extends single-agent survival across two independent adult orthotopic patient-derived backgrounds (GBM8 and G06); intraperitoneal CT-179 is associated with reduced intratumoral OLIG2 and Ki-67 staining in GBM8 tumors. Intraperitoneal CT-179 plus radiotherapy significantly extends survival in an MGMT-unmethylated GBM6 orthotopic model where temozolomide contributes minimally and supports the rationale for further evaluation in MGMT-unmethylated GBM. Importance of the Study Glioblastoma is uniformly fatal, and durable disease-modifying therapies that disable the lineage transcription factor programs sustaining the GBM stem-like state have remained elusive. OLIG2 is universally expressed in diffuse glioma and is a central driver of stemness, lineage-restricted RTK signaling, and resistance to genotoxic therapy, yet has historically been considered undruggable. This study reports the foundational preclinical characterization of CT-179, a brain-penetrant small molecule that engages OLIG2 directly and induces glioblastoma cell death through disrupted mitotic progression. Oral CT-179 crosses the blood-brain barrier, prolongs survival in orthotopic patient-derived xenografts, and substantially enhances the efficacy of standard-of-care radiotherapy and temozolomide. Activity in an MGMT-unmethylated orthotopic patient-derived GBM model in combination with radiotherapy is of particular translational interest, since this is the patient population for which temozolomide contributes minimally and the unmet need is greatest. These data establish proof of concept for direct pharmacologic inhibition of OLIG2 in GBM and provide a translational rationale, including an MGMT-stratified combination strategy, for combining CT-179 with current standard-of-care chemoradiotherapy. Lay Summary Glioblastoma is the most common and aggressive brain cancer in adults, and almost all patients die of their disease. One reason is a protein called OLIG2, which keeps tumor cells in an immature, treatment-resistant state and has long been considered impossible to target with drugs. We studied CT-179, a small molecule that enters the brain and blocks OLIG2. In glioblastoma cells and in mice, CT-179 forced dividing tumor cells into a faulty, lethal division, extended survival on its own, and strengthened the effect of standard radiation and chemotherapy. These results support testing CT-179 in people with glioblastoma.

title: Interictal functional ultrasound imaging in human epilepsy resection and responsive neurostimulation surgery
abstract: Over 30% of patients with epilepsy are refractory to medication and may require surgical or neuromodulation-based intervention. Accurate localization of seizure-onset zones (SOZ) and assessment of treatment-associated brain responses remain major clinical challenges. Current workflows may involve invasive intracranial monitoring, prolonged hospitalization, adjustment of anti-seizure medications, and seizure capture to localize the SOZ, while opportunities for complementary intraoperative functional assessment remain limited. We used intraoperative functional ultrasound imaging (fUSI) to characterize interictal (i.e., non-seizure) cortical activity in nine patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and to assess treatment-associated brain responses following SOZ resection and responsive neurostimulation (RNS). fUSI signals were acquired directly from the exposed cortex during standard-of-care surgery. We developed six ultrafast power Doppler-based interictal activity markers (IaMs) to distinguish SOZ from peri-resection zone (PRZ) cortex and to quantify treatment-associated changes. The IaMs revealed distinct interictal hemodynamic dynamics between SOZ and PRZ cortex. Following SOZ resection, all six markers changed significantly within the surrounding PRZ. RNS also induced robust, stimulation paradigm-dependent modulation of cortical hemodynamic dynamics. Notably, RNS and surgical resection produced concordant directional changes across five of the six IaMs, despite representing fundamentally different therapeutic interventions. Together, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of intraoperative fUSI for characterizing and distinguishing interictal dynamics within SOZ and PRZ cortex and assessing treatment-associated cortical responses during human epilepsy surgery. Furthermore, fUSI could provide a complementary high-resolution functional imaging approach alongside established clinical methods for SOZ localization and intraoperative functional assessment.

title: Claims-based reconstruction of the pancreatic cancer care pathway links centralization of care to survival
abstract: Background The organization of pancreatic cancer care may be associated with survival. Using health administrative claims data, we reconstructed the pathway from diagnosis to first-line therapy and examined associations of multidisciplinary team review and treatment at specialized centers with overall survival. Methods Longitudinal historical cohort study using anonymized health administrative claims data from six Czech health insurance funds, covering approximately 17% of patients diagnosed with pancreatic cancer nationally between 2018 and 2020. Adults with an incident ICD-10 C25 record confirmed by imaging and histopathology were followed from the index date (the date of the first qualifying imaging or histopathological examination) until death, censoring, or 31 December 2021. Overall survival was analyzed using Kaplan–Meier methods and Cox regression adjusted for age and first-line therapy type. Results Of 1,255 patients, 920 (73.3%) received first-line therapy and 266 (21.2%) died untreated. Among treated patients, 436 (47.4%) underwent multidisciplinary team review, 335 (36.4%) underwent surgery, and 667 (72.5%) were treated at a complex oncological center. Surgery was associated with longer overall survival than chemotherapy (age-adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 0.32, P < 0.001). Treatment at a complex oncological center was associated with longer overall survival (adjusted HR 0.77, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.64–0.92, P = 0.004; crude median 532 versus 394 days). Multidisciplinary team review was not significantly associated with overall survival (adjusted HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.73–1.01, P = 0.073). Conclusions Treatment at a complex oncological center was associated with longer survival, while fewer than half of patients had a recorded multidisciplinary team review. How care is organized, not only which therapy is delivered, is associated with outcome. The observational design and absence of key clinical covariates limit causal interpretation.

title: Morphometric Brain Networks at Ultra-Low Field: A First Assessment of Feasibility and Reliability
abstract: Background: Ultra-low field (ULF) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers accessible point-of-care neuroimaging, yet its capability to support multivariate network analyses remains understudied. Methods: We systematically evaluated the feasibility and reliability of Morphometric Similarity Networks (MSN) and Morphometric Inverse Divergence (MIND) networks derived from paired high-field (HF, 3T/1.5T) and ULF (64mT) scans in a primary cohort(N=23) and an independent replication cohort (N=19). We tested the impact of super-resolution processing, cortical parcellation granularity (Desikan-Killiany vs. Destrieux), and mesh resolution (fsnative vs. fsaverage5) on edge-level cross-scanner agreement (Lin's concordance correlation coefficient, CCC) and subject-level identifiability. Results: MIND networks demonstrated higher edge-level HF-ULF agreement (mean CCC = 0.95) and ULF reproducibility (mean CCC = 0.98) compared to MSNs (mean CCC = 0.86-0.87 and 0.91-0.94, respectively). In contrast, MSNs yielded higher subject-level differential identifiability across field strengths due to a broader distinction between within- and between-subject similarity. Reconstructing MIND networks on native high-resolution meshes (fsnative) maximised cross-scanner agreement, whereas coarser meshes and finer cortical parcellations enhanced individual network identifiability. Conclusions: Structural similarity networks can be reliably constructed from ULF MRI data. Optimal analytic choices depend on study objectives: MIND on native meshes maximises cross-scanner stability, whereas MSNs excel at preserving individual uniqueness, paving the way for globally scalable connectomic research.

title: Individual-level Structural Neuroimaging Biomarkers across the Psychosis Spectrum
abstract: ABSTRACT Background and Hypothesis Although psychotic disorders are characterized by widespread cortical thinning, translating these findings into individualized biomarkers remains challenging. Regional Vulnerability Index (RVI) and Neuroscore are candidate individual-level biomarkers that quantify the similarity between an individual’s structural brain pattern and generic psychosis-associated alterations. This study investigated cortical thickness (CT)-based RVI and Neuroscore, along with mean CT deviation from healthy individuals, across the psychosis spectrum. Study Design Using structural 3T MRI data from 289 participants (clinical high risk for psychosis [CHR], n=39; first episode psychosis [FEP], n=44, chronic psychosis [CP], n=86; healthy controls [HC], n=120), RVI, Neuroscore, and mean CT deviation (z) scores were computed from region-wise CT measures quantified using FreeSurfer v7.2. Group differences and associations with symptoms were evaluated. Study Results RVI and Neuroscore were significantly higher, and mean CT z-scores lower, in FEP and CP compared with CHR and HC, with moderate-to-large effect sizes (|Cohen’s d| = 0.55–1.15). No differences were observed between FEP and CP or CHR and HC. Indices were not associated with psychosis-spectrum symptom severity in the CHR, FEP, or CP groups. RVI ( r = −0.561, p < .001) and Neuroscore ( r = −0.997, p < .001) were strongly negatively correlated with the mean CT z-score. Conclusions CT-based RVI and Neuroscore appear to index established disease status but not risk status, while showing substantial overlap with mean CT deviation. These findings highlight the need to further refine these biomarkers through data-driven and multimodal approaches to improve their utility for risk and prognostic prediction.

title: Prevalence and Clinical Correlates of Coronary Perivascular Inflammation in an Asymptomatic Adult Primary Prevention Population: An Assessment of the CT-Derived Fat Attenuation Index Score (FAI-Score)
abstract: Background Coronary perivascular fat attenuation index score (FAI-Score) on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) quantifies vascular inflammation and predicts cardiac mortality in symptomatic cohorts. However, its prevalence, anatomical distribution, and clinical correlates in asymptomatic primary prevention populations remain uncharacterized. Methods In an IRB-approved prospective study across two clinical sites, 84 consecutive asymptomatic adults (mean age 53.7 ± 8.6 years; 63.1% men) with no prior coronary artery disease underwent screening CCTA and comprehensive clinical, metabolic, and biomarker profiling. AI-standardized FAI-Score was quantified across three epicardial vessels (LAD, LCx, RCA). High and very high perivascular inflammation were pre-specified as any vessel ≥75th and ≥90th percentiles, respectively. Luminal stenosis and plaque were graded using CAD-RADS 2.0. Results Elevated FAI-Score (≥75th percentile) was present in 42.9% of participants (36/84; 95% CI 32.8% - 53.5%), with 17.9% (15/84; 95% CI 11.1% - 27.4%) exhibiting very high inflammation (≥90th percentile). Multi-vessel inflammation was identified in 17.9% (15/84), with the RCA most frequently involved (≥90th percentile in 13.1%). Standard circulating biomarkers, including ApoB, non-HDL-C, HbA1c, and PREVENT-ASCVD 10-year risk showed no association with binary inflammation. Systemic hs-CRP (median 0.8 mg/L) exhibited an inverse correlation with maximum vessel FAI-Score (Spearman ρ=−0.27, p=0.014). Men demonstrated higher rates of elevated FAI-Score than women (52.8% vs. 25.8%, p=0.016; ≥90th percentile: 26.4% vs. 3.2%, p=0.007). title: Leapfrogging cancer diagnostics with AI: a mixed-methods assessment of implementation determinants in low- and middle-income countries
abstract: Introduction Cancer incidence is rising rapidly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where diagnostic pathology capacity is constrained. AI applied to routine histopathology could strengthen diagnostic capacity and offer leapfrogging potential by embedding AI into diagnostic systems as they are built up. However, without empirically identifying implementation determinants in LMIC cancer-diagnostic settings, AI solutions risk being poorly aligned with local constraints, limiting impact or exacerbating existing disparities. Methods We conducted an exploratory mixed-methods pilot study across three phases: 1) a structured survey characterising the diagnostic and technical landscape and AI priorities; 2) focus group discussions (FGDs) to inductively identify implementation determinants and 3) a second survey quantifying FGD-derived themes. Twelve physicians were purposively recruited (10 from LMIC, 2 from high-income countries for reference) and findings integrated through narrative triangulation. Results There was substantial heterogeneity in diagnostic and AI infrastructure that did not track consistently with country income classification. H&E staining was universally available, immunohistochemistry capacity was rudimentary at 7 of 10 sites and molecular testing absent or minimal at 6 of 10 sites. Whole-slide-imaging scanners were available at 8 of 10 sites, while graphical processing units, required for efficient AI inference, were available at only 4 of 10 sites. The participants would prioritise use of AI for cancer screening, cancer diagnosis, and biomarker prediction from H&E slides. Six implementation determinants were identified: AI literacy, governance frameworks, funding, evidence generation, clinical deployment, and collaboration. Financial constraints emerged as the dominant barrier across all determinants, and collaboration as an important enabling mechanism. Conclusion AI implementation readiness in LMIC cancer-diagnostic settings is highly heterogeneous and cannot be inferred from income classification, underscoring the need for institution-level assessment. Realising the leapfrogging potential of AI in this context requires coordinated progress across all determinants, with sustainable financing, and collaboration enabling the remaining determinants. Key messages What is already known on this topic? Cancer incidence is rising rapidly in LMICs, where diagnostic capacity and molecular testing capabilities are severely constrained. AI could alleviate gaps, yet evidence on implementation determinants for integrating AI into cancer diagnostics in these settings remains limited. What this study adds? AI implementation readiness varies substantially within LMIC settings and does not track with country income classification. Readiness is shaped by six implementation determinants: AI literacy, governance frameworks, funding, evidence generation, clinical deployment, and collaboration, with financial constraints as the dominant cross-cutting barrier. How this study might affect research, practice or policy? These findings support institution-level feasibility assessment over income-classification proxies and highlight the need for sustainable financing and collaboration as foundational prerequisites for AI implementation in cancer diagnostics in LMICs.

title: Optogenetic and sonogenetic pacing of unmodified cardiac tissue upon quick integration with specialized biological actuators
abstract: ABSTRACT Electrical stimulation for cardiac pacing has been in clinical use for 100 years and it is the current standard. Alternative scalable pacing methods that are contactless, with good spatial precision and can also be cell-selective are of interest for both in vitro and in vivo applications. Cardiac pacing by light or by ultrasound (US) can be achieved using optogenetic transduction of the tissue and by enhancing responsiveness to ultrasound. In this work we create specialized biological actuators (cell spheroids) out of generic human cells, modified optogenetically (using Channelrhodopsin2) and sonogenetically (using human Piezo1), guide them to a desired location to promote quick integration with unmodified cardiac syncytia within less than two hours. We quantify their ability to confer pacing by light or US and to entrain the native cardiac tissue, modeled here with human induced pluripotent stem cell derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) grown in monolayers, quasi-3D oriented microtissues or cell spheroids. Magnetic guidance (via magnetic nanoparticles) speeds up integration and facilitates positioning to optimize electrotonic load for pacing; size match and three-dimensional growth also accelerate integration. Computational modeling corroborates the possibility to pace by light and by US. Using optogenetically-gated US pulses (0.5 MHz), we show entrainment in voltage and calcium responses and identify the best performing configurations. Experiments reveal the potential role of Piezo1, esp. when activated with Yoda1. The approach is shown to work with physiologically relevant heart cells, such as human cardiac fibroblasts as optimized actuators, and therefore can be considered for in vivo applications as part of heart regeneration efforts. High-throughput cardiotoxicity testing and drug screening in vitro can directly benefit from deployment of such biological actuators.

title: Overuse and False Restraint in Large Language Model Recommendations for Choosing Wisely Scenarios.
abstract: Background The Choosing Wisely initiative made recommendations where screening, testing, or treatment may be overused, with caveats around appropriate use. Clinicians are increasingly using large language models (LLMs). Objective To evaluate whether commercial LLMs appropriately call for restraint or action from scenarios based on Choosing Wisely recommendations. Design Benchmark evaluation. Fifteen Choosing Wisely recommendations were used to develop 225 scenarios (per recommendation, 10 in which restraint was appropriate and 5 in which action was appropriate). Six commercial LLMs (3 runs each) generated 4050 responses to the 225 scenarios, using a prompt from the clinician perspective. Setting Production application programming interfaces of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google from February to March 2026. Participants No human participants were involved. Measurements Co-primary outcomes were the overuse rate (endorsing action when restraint was appropriate) and the false restraint rate (withholding an appropriate action). Results The rate of LLM-recommended overuse was 5.4% (95% CI, 0.6% to 12.2%); LLMs did not recommend overuse in 8 of 15 recommendations. Two recommendations accounted for most LLM-recommended overuse: thyroid ultrasound for an incidental subcentimeter nodule (overuse recommended in 42.8% of LLM responses) and routine electrocardiography in low-risk adults (overuse recommended in 28.3% of LLM responses). The LLMs recommended overuse in 0.6% to 3.3% of responses for the remaining 5 recommendations. False restraint was rare (0.6% [CI, 0.1% to 1.2%]), was absent for 11 of 15 recommendations, and was highest for prostate-specific antigen screening (3.3%). Limitations Single prompts without follow-up; a benchmark rather than real-world use; responses classified by LLM judge with physician adjudication. Findings may not extend to consumer-facing use. Conclusion The LLMs rarely withheld recommendations for treatment when it was appropriate. Overuse was concentrated in 2 recommendations. Primary funding source None.

title: Diffuse-Type Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor of the Flexor Hallucis Longus Tendon Sheath: A Case Report.
abstract: The synovium can be the primary site for the development of various benign or malignant tumors. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT), also known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath, is a benign but locally aggressive synovial neoplasm occurring in localized and diffuse forms. The localized form predominantly affects the hand, whereas the diffuse form mainly involves large joints; involvement of the flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath is rare. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the principal modality for demonstrating the hemosiderin deposits characteristic of this lesion, although histopathology remains necessary for definitive diagnosis. Surgical resection remains the standard treatment. We report the case of a 24-year-old man with 10 months of right ankle pain, related to a diffuse-type TGCT involving the flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath and adjacent ankle joints. Radiographs initially showed soft-tissue filling of Kager's triangle. Computed tomography arthrography demonstrated synovial thickening but was nonspecific; MRI then revealed the characteristic findings, and histopathology confirmed the diagnosis. This report aims to raise awareness of this rare location and its associated diagnostic pitfalls.

title: ACorD: Adaptive Correspondence Discovery for Medical Image Registration
abstract: Medical image registration is a fundamental task for aligning anatomical structures across images. Exhaustively searching for point-wise correspondences is prohibitively expensive in both computation and memory, particularly for high-resolution 3D medical images. Most recent learning-based methods directly predict correspondences in a coarse-to-fine manner, but often propagate intermediate estimates across scales without explicitly weighting correspondence evidence, which can allow coarse-scale errors to persist during refinement. To address these challenges, we propose ACorD, an adaptive correspondence discovery framework designed to mitigate error propagation with an attention-guided process. ACorD first predicts multiple potential correspondence candidates through Correlation-guided Cross-scale Offset Prediction (CCOP), which combines correlation maps as spatial matching priors with cross-scale features as global deformation context. Then, Multi-Head Deformable Aggregation (MHDA) aggregates these candidate correspondences using attention, producing a learned, non-uniform weighting over competing matches rather than treating them equally. The multi-head design further captures complementary deformation patterns, ensuring both global alignment and local precision. By integrating adaptive offset prediction with selective, attention-based aggregation of correspondence evidence, ACorD enables accurate deformation refinement. Extensive experiments on four public medical registration benchmarks demonstrate that adaptive correspondence discovery within a multi-scale refinement framework improves registration robustness across diverse anatomical structures.

title: Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient MCI Conversion Prediction
abstract: Allocating limited trainable capacity across convolutional layers is a central challenge in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of pretrained three-dimensional (3D) networks. We propose Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation, which jointly selects input- and output-channel ranks under a fixed adapter-parameter budget while preserving the spatial kernel modes. To guide rank selection, we learn task-specific proxy updates from downstream training data and approximate them using candidate Tucker rank pairs. A perturbation analysis bounds the output discrepancy between the fixed proxy network and its Tucker approximation in terms of layerwise reconstruction residuals, motivating residual-based allocation. We normalize each squared residual by the corresponding proxy-update energy to compare relative approximation errors across layers. Dynamic programming minimizes their sum under a global budget constraint that accounts for both channel factors and the Tucker core. This yields a globally optimal allocation over the specified candidate rank pairs. We evaluate the method on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort for predicting conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease within 36 months, using hippocampal segmentation pretraining. Across five random seeds, the proposed method achieves a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.7706, compared with 0.7239 for fixed-ratio Tucker adaptation and 0.7430 for full fine-tuning. The total number of trainable parameters is limited to approximately 0.618 million, accounting for only 1.45% of the full model. Adaptive Tucker rank allocation thus provides an effective approach to parameter-efficient transfer learning in 3D medical imaging.

title: How Robust Are Prognostic Radiomic Features? Comparing Selection Techniques on Pooled Glioblastoma Cohorts
abstract: Radiomic survival studies in glioblastoma report heterogeneous prognostic features, but how much of this stems from the methodology itself is rarely examined. We analysed the association of 463 radiomic, anatomical and clinical features from pre-treatment MRI with overall survival in 705 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma patients from three public cohorts, using three techniques: a log-rank test after median split, univariate Cox regression (both Benjamini-Hochberg corrected) and an XGBoost regressor interpreted with SHAP. The log-rank test selected 99 features, Cox regression 72 and SHAP its top 20; five were selected by all three: age, a peritumoural T2 texture feature, the number of connected peritumoural mask components and two image-level intensity maxima. The two survival tests shared 51 features, about half of the SHAP top 20 were also selected by either test, and where selections overlapped, effect directions agreed. Many selections were PyRadiomics diagnostic descriptors that are not restricted to tumour voxels. Analytical pipeline choices, including ranking method, pre-filtering and descriptor handling, can substantially influence which features appear prognostic.

title: XGLASS: X-Ray, Gaze and Language Assisted Slice Sequencing for CT Volumes
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) achieve remarkable performance on 2D medical images, such as X-rays or pathology images, while 3D VLMs that directly process CT/MRI volumes lag behind due to limited 3D training data and the predominance of 2D foundation architectures. To leverage powerful 2D VLMs for analyzing medical volumes, which contain hundreds of slices, it is therefore necessary to focus only on those few slices, which are diagnostically relevant. To enable such a prioritization, we propose XGLASS, a method that transfers medical expertise from 2D X-rays to 3D CT for task-aware slice prioritization. XGLASS uses disease-conditioned importance maps derived from language-aligned radiologist gaze on X-rays and spatially aligns them with coronal CT projections, bringing gaze priors and CT content into a shared 2D representation. The fused gaze-prior/CT projection is then used to predict a disease-specific ordering of axial slices, prioritizing diagnostically relevant slices. XGLASS significantly improves budgeted retrieval over 2D and 3D-native baselines, achieving a top-10 hit rate up to 75.9% for the best-performing disease. In practice, this means that after inspecting only the top 10 slices (4.17% of a 240-slice scan), XGLASS identifies a diagnostically relevant slice in more than 75% of cases. For downstream slice-wise finding classification, an XGLASS-selected 30-slice candidate set reduces model calls by 87.5% while improving F1 by 11.3 percentage points over all-slice inference, 4.2 points over the strongest 2D selector, and remains competitive with 3D-native selectors while requiring up to 130.8 times less time and 10.9 times less GPU memory per finding, supporting its use as a lightweight preselector for volumetric CT analysis. The code and pretrained checkpoint are available on https://github.com/michaelgloeckler/XGLASS.

title: TIM: Temporal Decoupling with Iterative Mutual-Refinement Model for Longitudinal Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) aims to translate medical images into diagnostic text, reducing radiologists' workload and standardizing clinical documentation. Nonetheless, existing approaches mainly focus on single-timepoint analysis and fail to capture temporal disease evolution across longitudinal examinations. While recent longitudinal RRG (LRRG) approaches incorporate historical data, they often combine images from different time points within a single representation space, leading to blurred semantics and inconsistent temporal reasoning. In this work, we propose a Temporal Decoupling with Iterative Mutual-Refinement Model (TIM), a two-stage framework that explicitly decouples spatial pathology from temporal progression and iteratively refines reports through mutual feedback. Stage I performs temporal-decoupled representation learning, separating temporal evolution patterns from disease-specific features and generating radiology reports for both prior and current studies. Stage II introduces a mutual report refinement mechanism that identifies diagnostic inconsistencies within prior reports and iteratively rectifies both prior and current reports through error-sensitive feedback. Experiments on the Longitudinal-MIMIC dataset demonstrate that TIM surpasses existing single-image and longitudinal baselines, achieving new state-of-the-art performance across both language and clinical metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/yihengd/TIM.

title: MCDA: Multi-View Graph Contrastive Learning with Dynamic Topology Augmentation for Functional MRI Analysis
abstract: Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) is a vital non-invasive tool for diagnosing brain disorders and uncovering pathological mechanisms. However, existing graph contrastive learning (GCL) methods often underexploit augmentation histories across training epochs and the relationships among different augmented views. In this paper, we introduce a topology-guided Multi-view graph Contrastive learning framework with Dynamic graph topology Augmentation (MCDA) for fMRI analysis. Unlike traditional GCL that uses fixed noise or edge-dropping, MCDA employs a Dynamic Augmentation Update (DAU) module that iteratively refines the augmented topology. Specifically, we incorporate self-aware and cross-sample augmentation strategies to simultaneously capture individual-specific functional signatures and inter-subject heterogeneity. We then design a topology-guided multi-view graph contrastive learning scheme that explores interrelationships not only between the original network and its augmented views, but also across different augmented views to maximize structural information preservation. We characterize the score-level optimization directions and establish a lower bound for the contrastive objective. The framework combines classification and contrastive losses for brain disorder diagnosis and examines discriminative functional connectivity patterns as potential biomarkers. Experiments on two public rs-fMRI datasets comprising 1,236 subjects demonstrate that MCDA outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. The code has been made publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/goodcodingagoodboy/MCDA}.

title: HGASurv: Hierarchical Granularity-Aware Multimodal Integration for Survival Prediction
abstract: Multimodal survival prediction jointly analyzes histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs), genomic profiles, and clinical variables to stratify patients by risk. However, existing approaches often inadequately account for granularity differences across modalities, particularly in spatial organization and feature dimensionality. Within pathology, aggregating WSI patch features without preserving their spatial arrangement can obscure tissue architecture; across modalities, directly concatenating low-dimensional clinical variables with high-dimensional visual and genomic features may limit the contribution of clinical information to prediction. To address these challenges, we propose HGASurv, which introduces a hierarchical WSI encoding module and a clinical-guided graph propagation module for granularity-aware multimodal integration. The hierarchical WSI encoding module maps WSI patch features onto a spatial grid using their original coordinates and applies parallel convolutions to construct representations at patch, local-neighborhood, and regional scales. Genomic signature embeddings then query these scale-specific WSI representations through cross-modal co-attention, producing signature-conditioned morphological features. The clinical-guided graph propagation module uses clinical variables to define patient-similarity edges and propagates fused image-genomic node embeddings with graph attention, integrating clinical information through topology rather than feature concatenation. Across three TCGA cohorts, HGASurv achieved the strongest overall C-index performance, with ablation studies supporting the complementary contributions of the hierarchical WSI encoding and clinical-guided graph propagation modules. This design shows that matching representation and integration mechanisms to modality-specific granularity improves multimodal survival prediction.

title: Progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory for incomplete multimodal brain tumor segmentation
abstract: Brain tumor segmentation uses complementary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequences, but some sequences may be unavailable in practice. Their absence changes the information available for segmenting different tumor regions. Fusion methods can support different input subsets. However, fusion at several scales does not by itself specify how tumor evidence is retained and updated to guide fusion at later stages. We propose a progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory network (PMTM) for segmentation from any non-empty subset of T1ce, T1, FLAIR, and T2. PMTM maintains a compact state for the current subject across the encoder stages. At each stage, we use assignment maps to pool spatial features into ordered evidence vectors for each available modality. We average these vectors across the available modalities, and a learned gate combines this evidence with the previous state. The up- dated state guides residual fusion at that stage and is used in the state update at the next stage. A modality-token mixer also models interactions among the available modalities at each stage. We apply semantic supervision to the assignment maps at all four stages. We evaluate PMTM on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI across all 15 non-empty modality subsets. Averaged over the three tumor regions and the 15 subsets, PMTM achieves Dice scores of 75.31%, 77.54%, and 80.47% on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI, respectively. These scores are higher than those of RobustSeg, RFNet, and mmFormer in our experiments on each dataset. Component ablations and internal state analysis are performed on BraTS2020.

title: 3D Diffusion Models for Medical Imaging
abstract: Generative deep learning methods such as Variational Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks or Diffusion Models have achieved remarkable results in image synthesis. In particular, Diffusion Models have demonstrated superior image fidelity and sample diversity compared to other approaches on standard benchmarks, while also offering more flexible training dynamics as evidenced both in natural image domains and in medical applications. In medical imaging including Computed Tomography, Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Positron Emission Tomography, such models have various important use-cases including data augmentation, domain transfer, image reconstruction, inpainting, image augmentation and artifact correction. Further, generated images can be conditioned on patient characteristics, medical reports, segmentation masks or other images. Specific challenges arise due to the 3D volumetric nature of medical images, which translate to substantial demands in terms of memory, compute, and training data. This article provides a comparative overview of 3D Diffusion Models which have been developed for medical images, with a focus on current performance, limitations, and an outlook for future work.

title: MRI Reconstruction Risk Estimation from Inference Dynamics
abstract: Iterative MRI reconstructors produce intermediate estimates before returning a final image. We study these inference trajectories as a model-internal representation of realized reconstruction risk, measured by log-NMSE. Model-native states are projected to magnitude images, summarized by a fixed 16-dimensional descriptor, and mapped to risk using a source-trained ridge readout. Across three reconstruction backbones, trajectory features are strongly predictive of reconstruction risk on held-out source data. Under zero-shot target shift, their behavior is backbone-dependent, exhibiting both preserved positive association and readout reversal. Conditional analyses show that trajectory information can remain associated with error beyond an initialization-only predictor. A prefix analysis further shows that useful trajectory information can emerge before reconstruction completes. Repeated-mask and low-shot calibration studies indicate that trajectories primarily encode persistent case difficulty, while their orientation and calibration can change under domain shift.

title: Scaling Vision Foundation Models for Toxicologic Pathology
abstract: Here, we present TOX-FM, a family of non-clinical PFMs trained on large-scale diverse histopathology datasets of over one million whole slide images consisting of over 60 organs across six animal species from over 14,000 toxicology studies across six decades. We introduce a comprehensive benchmark of 18 non-clinical downstream tasks, incorporate an established benchmark of 9 clinical downstream tasks, and evaluate TOX-FM against state-of-the-art clinical PFMs across both non-clinical and clinical domains. Notably, we explore open questions surrounding domain-specific training and cross-domain generalization, offering insights into the opportunities and challenges of applying PFMs in the non-clinical domain.

title: REST: Reliability-Guided Spatial Transcriptomics Supervision for Gene Expression Prediction from Histopathological HE-Stained Images
abstract: Histopathology is central to cancer diagnosis, but morphology in Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE)-stained images does not directly reveal the molecular states that characterize disease heterogeneity and inform tumor characterization, prognostic assessment, and biomarker discovery. Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) measures spatially resolved gene expression, providing molecular information within tissue architecture, yet differences in assay coverage and spot informativeness make paired HE--ST observations unequally reliable for representation learning. We propose Reliability-Guided Spatial Transcriptomics (REST) supervision with Biological Program Bank (BPB), a program-structured and reliability-guided ST-supervised training framework for predicting molecular information from H\&E images. REST constructs BPB from curated signature, pathway, and cell-type gene sets to provide a shared structure for ST encoding, reliability estimation, and molecular reconstruction. Guided by BPB, Spot-Reliability Contrastive Alignment (SRCA) measures the reliability of each spot from assay-level program coverage and spot-level activity dispersion, and reweights HE--ST alignment accordingly. Biology-Informed Program Reconstruction (BIPR) further uses learnable program queries to reconstruct member-gene expression from histological morphology. REST's training corpus comprised 209 samples (407,475 spots across 16 organs); evaluation used 70 disjoint samples (230,056 spots across eight organs) for gene-expression, pathway-activity, and cell-signature prediction. REST achieved the highest Macro correlation among state-of-the-art ST-supervised training methods and outperformed existing pathology foundation models. Code is available at https://github.com/lanfz2000/REST.

title: MoSAIK: Motion Search with Artificial Intelligence in K-space
abstract: Object: Motion artefacts remain a major limitation of routine two-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) brain MRI, reducing diagnostic confidence and often necessitating repeated acquisitions. MoSAIK (Motion Search with AI in K-space) retrospectively estimates in-plane rigid-body motion directly from standard multi-coil TSE k-space. Without a motion-free reference, external navigators, or additional acquisitions, MoSAIK infers motion from k-space self-consistency violations and incorporates predicted parameters into model-based, motion-aware reconstruction rather than synthesizing corrected images. Materials and Methods: Selected complex coil data were represented as log-magnitude and phase channels. A decoupled convolutional embedding and Transformer encoder estimated phase-encoding-line-indexed rotation and two-dimensional translations. Training used motion-free clinical acquisitions with simulated motion; four held-out subjects were evaluated. Component-wise errors assessed estimation; SSIM and PSNR in silico and entropy focus criterion (EFC) in vivo assessed reconstruction. Results: Motion estimation errors were low for both rotation (MSE $<$ 0.2 deg$^2$) and translation (MSE $<$ 0.2 pixels$^2$), with Pearson correlations of approximately 0.96 and 0.94, respectively. In every in-vivo acquisition, more than 75% of slices showed information gain relative to uncorrected reconstructions. MoSAIK reduced visible artefacts while preserving anatomical detail. Discussion: Transformer-based k-space motion-trajectory estimation enables fast retrospective correction of standard clinical TSE brain MRI.

title: Computer-Assisted Hip Arthroscopy for Portal Establishment and Suture Anchor Placement.
abstract: Hip arthroscopy is the gold standard for treating femoroacetabular impingement syndrome and acetabular labral tears. Portal establishment and suture anchor placement are crucial steps for ensuring the success of the surgery. However, because of the complex anatomy, deep location, and narrow joint space of the hip joint, the learning curve for establishing the hip arthroscopy approach and placing suture anchors for labral repair is arduous, with a high risk of iatrogenic cartilage and labral damage. This article describes a solution that applies computer-assisted navigation to these 2 key steps. Based on the patient's preoperative computed tomography data, this technique enables the reconstruction of an individualized 3-dimensional skeletal model, on which the clockface target of the anterolateral portal at the acetabular rim and the placement sites of suture anchors for labral repair are precisely planned. Intraoperatively, high-precision spatial registration between the preoperative virtual plan and the patient's actual anatomical structure is achieved via 2-dimensional to 3-dimensional image registration. With the assistance of the navigation system, the surgeon can accurately establish the arthroscopic portal in a single attempt without fluoroscopy and safely perform acetabular suture anchor placement for subsequent labral suture.

title: Retained Colorectal Foreign Body After Suspected Chemical Incapacitation: A Surgical and Forensic Challenge.
abstract: Retained rectal foreign bodies are an uncommon but clinically significant surgical emergency. We report the case of a 74-year-old male with multiple medical comorbidities who presented with progressive rectal pain and obstipation several days after an episode of suspected drug-facilitated assault. Plain radiography identified a large metallic aerosol can, and attempts to retrieve it under general anesthesia using surgical clamps and a magnetic probe failed. Intraoperative fluoroscopy demonstrated that the can had migrated proximal to the rectosigmoid junction into the left colon, precluding transanal extraction. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy with longitudinal colotomy, permitting safe removal of the foreign body without evidence of perforation or visceral injury. This case illustrates the critical role of intraoperative fluoroscopy when digital examination fails, the indications for operative intervention in proximally migrated foreign bodies, and the importance of considering drug-facilitated assault as an etiology.

title: Progressive Hippocampal Volume Reduction Beyond Normal Aging in Temporal Lobe Epilepsy: A Longitudinal MRI Study.
abstract: Recent neuroimaging studies have suggested that epilepsy may show progressive brain structural changes over time. However, longitudinal hippocampal volume changes in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) have not been adequately compared with those observed in normal aging. In this study, we enrolled 46 patients with unilateral TLE and 25 healthy controls with longitudinal structural MRI scans using the same scanner. Hippocampal volumes were quantified using the Hipposeg software, and the annual percentage volume reduction relative to baseline (%Reduction/year) was calculated for each hippocampus. Compared to healthy hippocampi (median -0.37% per year, IQR = 3.97), both ipsilateral (median -1.04% per year, IQR = 3.65) and contralateral (median -1.08% per year, IQR = 3.17) hippocampi in TLE showed significantly greater volume reduction over time (both p < 0.05). Furthermore, annual ipsilateral hippocampal volume reduction was significantly correlated with disease duration (Spearman's rs = 0.366, FDR-corrected p = 0.036), suggesting that hippocampal atrophy progresses more rapidly during the early stage after epilepsy onset. These findings indicate that hippocampal volume loss in TLE exceeds that expected from normal aging and provide further evidence supporting progressive structural alterations during the course of the disease. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Temporal lobe epilepsy may cause progressive changes in the brain beyond those expected from normal aging. Using repeated MRI scans, we found that the hippocampus showed greater volume loss over time in people with temporal lobe epilepsy than in healthy individuals. This volume loss occurred bilaterally and appeared to be greater during the earlier stages of the disease. These results provide further evidence supporting progressive structural brain changes in TLE and contribute to a better understanding of disease progression and abnormal brain aging in epilepsy.

title: Newly diagnosed and relapsed follicular lymphoma: EHA Clinical Practice Guidelines for diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up.
abstract: Follicular lymphoma (FL) is the second most common lymphoma subtype in Europe, with a median age at diagnosis of 60-65 years. It is generally considered an indolent disease, and the median overall survival at diagnosis now likely exceeds 20 years. However, considerable heterogeneity exists. Diagnosis requires adequate biopsy material and a specialized hematopathologist. Staging and prognosis rely on positron emission tomography (PET)-computed tomography (CT). Prognostication at diagnosis is based on several validated clinical prognostic scores. Localized disease is usually treated with radiotherapy ± Rituximab. The treatment of disseminated disease includes active surveillance (or in selected cases Rituximab monotherapy) for low-tumor burden patients, and most often immunochemotherapy (or in selected cases chemo-free therapeutic options), ±antibody maintenance in high-tumor burden patients. For relapsed or refractory disease, treatment with Rituximab-Lenalidomide combination ± Tafasitamab or Epcoritamab from the first relapse and single-agent bispecific antibodies, chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy (CAR-T) cells, and Zanubrutinib-Obinutuzumab after second relapse should be prioritized over immunochemotherapy. Given the long natural history and risk of relapse, careful follow-up is an important part of patient management. Patients should be actively involved in decision-making. In this guideline, we present current evidence-based recommendations for diagnosis, staging, treatment, and follow-up.
